documents.abstract: This paper introduces and analyzes a rare, intact pair of white-ground black-painted meiping (plum vases) from the Yuan Dynasty, specifically dated to the 2nd year of the Dade era (1298 CE). Preserved continuously as a unified diptych (SG-CZ-32 and SG-CZ-33) within the Sigong Collection, these vessels provide definitive epigraphic and physical evidence of individual authorship and advanced workshop ergonomics in late 13th-century Northern Chinese Cizhou kilns. Through a comparative analysis of the dual inscriptions (Dade Er Nian Feng Xiao Si Bi and Dade Er Nian Feng Si Bi), this study establishes the intentional alternate use of humilific prefixes (Xiao) by the same master artisan, Feng Si. Furthermore, macro-physical analysis of identical manual four-finger immersion glazing ("dumping method") marks on the foot rims offers unprecedented anthropological insight into the physical gestures of medieval Chinese ceramic production. Rather than a standard commercial product or a rigid institutional commission, this study concludes that the pair represents Feng Si’s self-actualized Magnum Opus, capturing a frozen cinematic record of individual artistic pride 728 years ago. Keywords: Cizhou Ware, Yuan Dynasty Ceramics, Meiping, Dated Inscription, Artisan Feng Si, Immersion Glazing, Literati Aesthetics, Sigong Collection

Abstract Product packaging has evolved from a purely functional necessity into a strategic marketing tool that actively shapes how consumers perceive, trust, and ultimately purchase a product. This study examines the influence of packaging on consumer purchasing decisions through a structured survey of 70 valid respondents, supported by a review of existing academic literature and a real-world business case study. The research finds that packaging measurably affects attention, trust, and purchase intent: 44.9% of respondents said attractive packaging genuinely catches their attention, 46.4% said good packaging builds trust, and 46.4% said poor packaging would strongly discourage a purchase. When shown two identical products differing only in packaging quality, with no price attached, 65.7% of respondents chose the better-packaged option, indicating that packaging alone carries substantial purchasing weight. Design and layout emerged as the single most valued packaging element (31.4%), ahead of material, eco-friendliness, product information, shape, and colour. A supporting case study of Tropicana's 2009 packaging redesign illustrates the commercial risk of poor packaging decisions, with the brand experiencing an estimated 20% sales decline within two months of an unrecognisable redesign. The study also explores how artificial intelligence is beginning to reshape packaging design, testing, and quality control. The study concludes that packaging is not a cosmetic afterthought but a measurable, quantifiable driver of consumer behaviour, and offers practical recommendations for businesses seeking to use packaging as a competitive tool.

At present, there are some problems in college English writing teaching, such as students ' low interest in writing, lack of personalized guidance, and low feedback efficiency. Artificial intelligence technology provides new ideas for teaching reform. In order to explore the actual impact of artificial intelligence-assisted teaching on college students’ English writing ability, this study selected two non-English major classes in Hubei Polytechnic University to carry out a one-semester quasi-experiment: 55 students in the experimental group adopted artificial intelligence-assisted teaching, and 53 students in the control group adopted traditional teaching. After the experiment, data were collected through questionnaires and in-depth interviews (10 students in each group), and the teaching effectiveness was evaluated by combining quantitative and qualitative results. The results showed that the average scores of each dimension of writing ability in the experimental class were higher than those in the control group, but did not reach a statistically significant level (P > 0.05). In the interview, the students in the experimental class had a significantly higher positive evaluation of writing interest (80%), learning effect (70%) and classroom interaction (90%). At the same time, they also put forward the problems of imperfect AI tools and easy to produce technical dependence. The control group feedback that the traditional teaching has the shortcomings of feedback lag and single form. In summary, although there is no significant statistical difference in the quantitative data, the mean value shows a positive trend of AI-assisted teaching, and the interview results also confirm that it can stimulate writing interest and improve learning experience. The teaching mode has application potential, and the teaching effect can be improved by prolonging the intervention cycle, optimizing the tools and strengthening the guidance of teachers.

The technical evolution of Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) has profoundly influenced the AI community, reshaping how intelligent systems understand, reason, and interact in both the digital and physical worlds. Through large-scale multimodal pretraining, MLLMs lay the foundation for general perception and alignment, while it remains unclear how such models can be transformed into human-grounded behaviors. Multimodal Post-Training, which further refines pretrained MLLMs to align their behaviors with human intent and real-world task demands, has become an important paradigm for advancing multimodal intelligence. Accordingly, both academia and industry have devoted increasing efforts to this direction, pushing the boundaries of multimodal general intelligence at an unprecedented pace. In this survey, we systematically review existing MMPoT research from a behavior-shaping perspective. Guided by this view, we introduce a unified framework that organizes existing MLLMs post-training methods into five major families: instruction following, preference calibration, reasoning enhancement, domain adaptation, and scalable learning. Moreover, we revisit benchmarks and evaluation protocols to critically assess the capabilities and limitations of post-trained MLLMs. To conclude, we provide a synthesized outlook on broader open questions, and highlight future research directions toward more general and reliable multimodal capabilities. An updated paper list is available at: https://github.com/zchoi/Awesome-post-training-for-MLLMs.

Blockchain architectures increasingly rely on smart contracts as programmable execution components, yet the security challenges they introduce remain only partially addressed. Fuzz testing has emerged as one of the leading automated techniques for smart contract vulnerability discovery; however, a systematic treatment linking classical fuzzing concepts to the specific architectural constraints of smart contract execution environments has remained elusive. We conduct a large-scale systematic review of 258 publications collected from Scopus and Google Scholar. The review is structured around four research questions covering general fuzzing limitations, EVM execution constraints, cross-contract interaction challenges, and technique transferability. The contributions are fourfold. First, we develop a conceptual taxonomy establishing an explicit correspondence between classical and smart contract fuzzing. Second, we present an architectural taxonomy of representative fuzzers unified under a generalised waypoint architecture that exposes key feedback domains and composition gaps. Third, we provide a categorised technique review spanning coverage-guided, hybrid, and learning-based approaches. Fourth, we offer a reproducibility critique with a structured research roadmap. Coverage-guided greybox fuzzing emerges as the dominant paradigm (51.2% of the 121 SC fuzzer tools); learning-based approaches (machine learning, reinforcement learning, and LLMs) are a small but emerging class, with LLM-guided fuzzing the fastest-emerging subcategory by recency. Feedback-domain composition remains sparse: most surveyed fuzzers combine only a few of the eight identified feedback domains, and none approaches the full set, leaving several high-value multi-domain compositions unexplored. Open challenges include scalable stateful exploration, standardised benchmarks and oracles, and EVM-specific architectural optimisations. The complete categorised corpus, coding, and search strategy are openly available.

The rapid evolution of digital technologies necessitates a transformative approach to accounting education, particularly in developing countries. Building on Mishra and Koehler’s (2006) foundational assertion that there is no universally accepted method for integrating technology into the educational curricula, this study proposes a TPACK-Bloom’s Taxonomy framework to articulate how technology enhances learning in accounting education. TPACK (Technological Pedagogical Content Knowledge) offers a multidimensional lens for aligning technological tools with pedagogical strategies and disciplinary content, ensuring that emerging technologies such as artificial intelligence and data analytics are contextually and instructionally relevant. Bloom’s Taxonomy complements this by structuring cognitive development across six hierarchical levels, ranging from remembering to creating, within technology-enhanced learning environments. Together, these two frameworks provide a versatile tool for designing curriculum interventions that foster digital literacy, critical thinking, and professional competence. This study makes three key contributions to the literature. First, it bridges the gap between technology adoption and pedagogical effectiveness by linking digital tools to cognitive learning outcomes. Second, it contributes to human capital development by promoting the integration of technical, cognitive, and digital competencies. Third, it supports organisational transformation by offering a practical, scalable approach to technology-enhanced learning in resource-constrained contexts.

Recent advances in large-scale foundation models have enabled strong generalization across a wide range of clinical and research tasks in magnetic resonance imaging (MRI). However, existing vision-language MRI models remain limited in anatomy-specific localization and pathology-aware representation, particularly in real-world settings. We introduce A4-MR, a 3D vision-language foundation model trained on approximately 50,000 MRI studies comprising 491,000 series, roughly half of which are paired with radiology reports. A4-MR is designed to: (1) learn anatomy localization through large-scale pretraining with noisy labels; (2) align image and text representations at the anatomical level; and (3) learn distinct representations of healthy and abnormal anatomy. Across a diverse set of downstream tasks, A4-MR outperforms existing foundation models, including a +1.7 AUROC improvement over MedSigLIP for abnormality detection. Using a frozen encoder, A4-MR also surpasses an end-to-end task-specific MedNeXt model for knee segmentation by +1.4 Dice and performs comparably to the best task-specific model for abdominal organ segmentation on AMOS, within 0.4 Dice. Finally, without anatomical prompts, A4-MR localizes 3D anatomy comparably to MedSAM2 provided with ground-truth bounding boxes. Together, these results demonstrate that anatomy-level multimodal alignment and abnormality-aware representation learning can enable a single MRI foundation model to support localization, segmentation, and pathology-related tasks.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into higher education, yet little is known about how students’ achievement goal orientations are associated with their engagement in AI-supported learning. Grounded in Achievement Goal Theory, this study examined the relationships among mastery-approach, mastery-avoidance, performance-approach, and performance-avoidance goals, enjoyment, flow, and student engagement. Survey data were collected from 662 Chinese university students with experience in AI-supported learning. Structural equation modeling was employed to examine psychological pathways, while fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis was used to identify alternative configurations associated with high engagement. The results showed that both mastery goals were positively associated with enjoyment and flow, whereas both performance goals were associated with flow but not enjoyment. Enjoyment mediated the relationships between mastery goals and engagement, while flow mediated the relationships between all four goal orientations and engagement. The configurational analysis further identified multiple sufficient pathways to high engagement, with no single condition being necessary. These findings extend Achievement Goal Theory by revealing differentiated affective and immersive mechanisms and multiple motivational configurations underlying student engagement in AI-supported higher education.

While reinforcement learning with verifiable reward (RLVR) enhances reasoning in large language models, its efficacy in long-horizon multimodal tasks remains underexplored. Visual Sudoku puzzles pose a representative challenge, requiring multi-step deductive reasoning over both local constraints and global dependency chains. To this end, we introduce FG-Sudoku, a fine-grained benchmark categorized by grid size and required deductive steps. Evaluations reveal that frontier MLLMs fail on complex long-range dependencies (e.g., 9*9 puzzles). During post-training, this near-zero success rate causes severe reward sparsity, halting standard RLVR. We propose Adaptive Curriculum Group Relative Policy Optimization (AdaC-GRPO) to overcome this. Unlike rigid or prior-based schedules, AdaC-GRPO dynamically constructs training batches by tracking the model's "Zone of Proximal Development" via online rollout accuracy. Experiments demonstrate that AdaC-GRPO enables Qwen2.5-VL-7B to approach the performance of Gemini-2.5-Flash while bridging 62.2% of the overall accuracy gap to Gemini-2.5-Pro, with its generalizability further validated across InternVL-3.5 and Qwen3-VL.

This thesis explores the role of adaptive digital learning technologies in teaching English for Specific Purposes (ESP). It examines how digital platforms, artificial intelligence, learning analytics, and personalized learning systems can address students' individual needs, language proficiency levels, and professional goals. Particular attention is given to the development of specialized vocabulary, professional communication skills, and learner autonomy. The thesis also discusses the benefits and challenges of implementing adaptive technologies in higher education. It argues that the effective integration of adaptive digital tools into ESP instruction can improve learning flexibility, engagement, and the relevance of language education to students' future professional activities.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: Introduction This study examines the adoption of AI digital humans (AI-DHs) by agricultural regional public brands in short-video promotion. Methods A complex network evolutionary game model is developed in which brands interact on a scale-free network and update their strategies through the Fermi rule. The model considers AI-DH production and generation costs, real-human promotion costs, consumer preference, recommendation priority, and network size. For each parameter scenario, 100 stochastic simulation runs are conducted, and mean adoption trajectories with 95% simulation intervals are reported. Results Higher AI-DH-related costs reduce the relative payoff of AI-DH promotion and suppress adoption, whereas higher real-human promotion costs make AI-DH promotion comparatively more attractive. Consumer preference produces the most pronounced change in the evolutionary outcome, with higher preference shifting the system toward broader AI-DH adoption. Higher recommendation priority helps sustain AI-DH adoption during the evolutionary process but does not independently determine the final adoption state. Network size has limited influence on long-run average adoption, although larger networks reduce stochastic variation in the evolutionary process. Discussion These findings extend digital-human research from post-adoption consumer responses to the dynamic adoption decisions of agricultural regional public brands and highlight the roles of relative payoffs, platform conditions, and inter-brand learning.

Diagnostic imaging of the oral and maxillofacial region is of paramount importance in clinical diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up procedures in dentistry. Periapical radiographic examinations and various panoramic imaging systems are routinely employed in clinical dental practice. Cone-beam computed tomography (CBCT) has become a widely used and currently preferred imaging modality in dental implantology, endodontics, maxillofacial surgery, periodontology, temporomandibular joint disorders, orthodontics, airway assessment, sleep disorders, and forensic dentistry. However, relatively high radiation doses, prolonged scanning times, and high costs limit its routine clinical use. Ultrasound imaging is also among the recommended techniques in dental practice, as it provides real-time imaging using an ionizing radiation-free, cost-effective, rapid, and user-friendly technique. Ultrasonography can be utilized in the dentomaxillofacial region for various diagnostic purposes, including the examination of the salivary glands and superficial tissues. More recently, dedicated dental magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has been introduced, incorporating specialized software, hardware, imaging sequences, and fields of view tailored to the anatomical characteristics of the dentomaxillofacial region. Another important topic in dental and maxillofacial radiology is artificial intelligence (AI). Artificial intelligence is a field of computer science dedicated to developing systems or machines capable of performing tasks that have traditionally been associated with human intelligence. Further research and investigation in the field of dental and maxillofacial radiology are expected to make substantial contributions to diagnostic imaging across various dental specialties. This article provides insights into current applications and emerging trends in the field of diagnostic imaging in dentistry.

A go-kart is a small, lightweight four-wheeled vehicle designed for recreational, educational and competitive driving. This project deals with the design and fabrication of a go-kart powered by an internal combustion (IC) engine. The main objective is to develop a simple, strong, economical and serviceable vehicle using commonly available mechanical components and workshop processes. The project covers the selection of the IC engine, chassis design, steering system, braking system, power transmission, wheels and tyres, accelerator and control mechanism. The frame is designed to support the engine, driver and other components while maintaining adequate rigidity and stability. The engine converts the chemical energy of fuel into mechanical power, which is transmitted to the driving axle through a suitable transmission arrangement. The methodology includes requirement identification, conceptual design, component selection, basic engineering calculations, CAD/drawing preparation, material procurement, fabrication, assembly and testing. The report also discusses important safety aspects such as braking performance, steering response, chain guarding, fastener tightening and driver protection. The project provides practical understanding of automobile engineering, IC engines, manufacturing processes, machine design, welding, power transmission and vehicle testing. The final design can be further improved by reducing weight, improving ergonomics, optimizing power transmission and introducing additional safety and instrumentation.

Emotion is a fundamental component of human communication, shaping understanding, trust, and engagement across domains such as education, healthcare, and mental health. Although large language models (LLMs) exhibit strong reasoning and knowledge-generation capabilities, they still struggle to express emotions in a consistent, controllable, and contextually appropriate manner. This limitation restricts their potential for authentic human–AI interaction. We propose a controllable emotion generation framework based on Emotion Vectors (EVs) —latent representations derived from internal activation shifts between neutral and emotion-conditioned responses. By injecting these vectors into the hidden states of pretrained LLMs during inference, our method enables fine-grained, continuous modulation of emotional tone without any additional training or architectural modification. We further provide a first-order theoretical analysis of emotional steering and its interaction with a semantic readout under explicit local assumptions. Experiments across multiple LLM families demonstrate adjustable emotional expression and characterize the model-dependent trade-off between steering strength, topical relevance, and fluency. The framework provides a general, training-free control interface with explicit intensity scaling and vector composition. Comparisons with prompting and fine-tuning characterize the emotional and quality effects of the evaluated configurations. Emotion Vector (EV) steering thus offers an efficient and interpretable means of bridging rational reasoning and affective understanding in large language models, and points to a promising direction for building emotionally resonant AI systems capable of more natural human–machine interaction.

Mobile ad hoc networks (MANETs) that operate in environments where energy harvesting takes place are confronted with three constant routing impediments: temporal blindness when predicting when energy will deplete, overestimation of link stability due to user mobility, and a lack of topological awareness resulting in fragile route selection. To address these issues, we propose adaptive fuzzy graph temporal network (AFGT-Net), an all-inclusive artificial intelligence (AI) based routing structure that comprises an long short-term memory (LSTM) model to predict the availability of future energy based on the past availability of energy; a Mamdani-type fuzzy inference system to support uncertainty-based decision-making by weighting different factors when making routing decisions; and multiple graph attention networks (multi-headed GATs) to support topological sensitivity in the routing decision process. A joint model was created to improve energy dynamics, mobility uncertainly, and structural robustness through joint training. Experiments were performed with physics-based simulations created in Python and network simulations created with NS-3 (v3.40) respectively. The experimental results revealed that AFGT-Net achieved an overall packet delivery ratio (PDR) of 89.6% while reducing the root mean squared error (RMSE) for energy prediction to be 0.052 joules and was able to extend the route lifetime (TR) by 1.62 times compared to baseline routing protocols. When compared to other AI (i.e.: GNN-R, DRL-R, and FedMANET) based routing protocols, the results demonstrated a consistent increase in all three throughput, delay and energy efficiency metrics. The proposed framework has been developed to provide a scalable and robust IoT network, disaster response system and future 6G wireless environment.

AI agents increasingly execute written instructions (SOPs, rulebooks, approval policies, or simply the prompt) to make consequential decisions at scale: a customer-service bot applies a reimbursement SOP; a clinical assistant executes a triage protocol. When two rules jointly create an impossible obligation, agents following them fail systematically. No alignment technique or behavioral monitor can fix a contradiction that lives in the instructions themselves. We present AGENTCOMPILER, a neuro-symbolic auditor that checks instructions before any agent executes them, a compile-time concer distinct from runtime compliance. An LLM extracts typed rules; deterministic detectors enumerate structural candidates; Lean 4 artifacts gate PROVEN verdicts; failures fall closed to human review. Extraction-dependent findings remain review hypotheses. We release a benchmark of 102 singleand 20 mixed-defect mutations over 48 public procedure documents with a 12-type taxonomy and independent construct audit. On the five formally verifiable defect classes, AGENTCOMPILER achieves F1 = 0.904 (P = 0.945, R= 0.867, FPR = 0.055), outperforming LLM baselines (F1 = 0.75–0.83, FPR up to 0.69), and reaches micro-F1 = 0.833 on mixed-defect documents. Detection is fully deterministic across repeated runs. Formal checking can make an extracted subclaim replayable; it cannot by itself certify the source procedure.

Computational fluid dynamics (CFD) workflows remain strongly dependent on expert decisions in geometry preparation, meshing, model and solver configuration, convergence assessment, post-processing, and design iteration. This review examines agentic artificial intelligence (AI) for CFD automation and engineering design, with emphasis on reinforcement learning (RL) agents and large language model (LLM) agents. RL agents provide rapid, task-specific, and physics-aware execution within predefined observation and action spaces, whereas LLM agents offer flexible goal interpretation, knowledge access, planning, and tool orchestration. To organize these potentially complementary capabilities, a unified taxonomy is introduced based on decision paradigm, CFD role, and degree of autonomy, while multi-agent organization is treated as a separate architectural property. The reviewed evidence indicates that neither RL nor LLM agents alone are sufficient for trustworthy autonomous CFD. A hierarchical autonomous-CFD-engineer architecture is therefore proposed, combining an LLM orchestrator, domain-specialized agents, conventional CFD tools, independent numerical and physical verification, shared provenance, and human governance. Extending this architecture toward hypothesis formulation, numerical-experiment design, and model discovery suggests a pathway to an AI CFD scientist; however, current systems support bounded automation and supervised scientific collaboration rather than independent scientific judgment.

topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have taken the world by storm. Their ability to communicate with us in our own language, and to reason about our world, has made them a favorite tool for writing, answering questions, and much more. Their answers already influence our decisions and our actions. What would happen if LLMs themselves could act in the world directly? What would happen if LLMs could interact with each other? Agentic LLMs combine the power of large language models with the ability to act in the real world. In this book we will discuss how agentic LLMs work, how they act, how they interact, and what this means for us, as users.

Tool-using agents increasingly require a common substrate for building, training, evaluating, distilling, and maintaining agentic systems, yet existing tooling typically addresses these stages in isolation. We present AgentTune, a source-available Python library that provides a unified framework for developing and optimizing tool-using agents. At its core, AgentTune introduces a two-tier EventLog representation that preserves agent trajectories while supporting consistent projections for training, evaluation, and auditing. Building on this substrate, the library provides a shared agent runtime, tool-calling reinforcement learning, agentic distillation, retrieval-augmented generation, decision workflows, evaluation utilities, and a designed path toward self-healing agents. These components are exposed through composable interfaces so that agent strategies, training methods, evaluation procedures, and recovery mechanisms can be combined without requiring separate representations or pipelines. We demonstrate the framework across agentic tasks including legal contract search and domain-specific applications, illustrating its use for trajectory-based optimization, tool-use evaluation, and cross-task agent development. AgentTune is released as a source-available library at https://github.com/Lexsi-Labs/AgentTune

AI agents increasingly select and pay service providers without human review. In emerging permissionless markets, however, adversaries can create inexpensive identities and fabricate feedback to inflate provider reputation, making reputation-based payment authorization vulnerable to Sybil attacks and exposing clients to unbounded financial loss. This paper presents AgentValve, a protocol for Sybil-resilient payment authorization in permissionless AI markets. AgentValve builds on a trust network that represents reputation as finite capacity in a directed graph and authorizes payments through trust paths with sufficient available capacity. A smart contract atomically reserves the capacity supporting each admitted payment, bounding honest agents' payment exposure by the capacity they extend into the adversarial region, and thus creating identities or interactions entirely within that region cannot increase this bound. To limit capacity depletion by malicious senders, AgentValve combines payment-backed capacity creation with bounded route length, preventing attackers from depleting honest capacity without incurring corresponding payment costs. AgentValve further decouples off-chain route discovery from on-chain verification and introduces a witness-commit mechanism that reduces route verification to linear work while requiring only constant persistent state per admitted payment. We implement a AgentValve prototype and evaluate it using six months of Ethereum data and synthetic workloads. Experimental results show that under attacks with up to 10,000 synthetic Sybil identities and with chosen attackers, the payment exposure and capacity depletion remain bounded. Regarding practicality, the witness-commit mechanism lowers admission cost by up to 40.8% compared with baselines, and admitting common payments costs approximately \$0.04-\$0.21.

LLM judges are increasingly deployed as panels, and disagreement among panel members is often read as a symptom of an unclear rubric. We test a label-free procedure that turns this disagreement into rubric repairs. The procedure decomposes each rubric into sub-criteria, ranks them by cross-judge disagreement on a development split, and has an editor model rewrite only the most contested ones. An additional stage that moves text-checkable sub-criteria to deterministic checkers transferred none in our evaluation. Human labels are never used to select or edit clauses; they are used only to evaluate the outcome. We pre-specified four hypotheses in a version-controlled protocol and evaluated six rubric conditions with a panel of five judges from three providers on SummEval, the HealthBench meta-evaluation, and USR Topical-Chat, for a total of 129,770 judge requests, excluding retries. On SummEval, the procedure raised inter-judge Krippendorff's $α$ by 0.069 (95% CI 0.046 to 0.092) over the original rubric and by 0.074 over a control that applied the same edits to an equal number of randomly chosen clauses that were not selected. Agreement with expert ratings showed no detectable change (Kendall $τ$ difference -0.007, 95% CI -0.037 to 0.021). On HealthBench and USR, neither inter-judge agreement nor human agreement met the preregistered effect criteria. In a preregistered secondary comparison, human agreement after editing the contested clauses was lower than after editing the control clauses on all three datasets in point estimate, although no interval excluded zero. Selecting clauses by disagreement makes judges agree with each other more than editing arbitrary clauses does, but in our setting the added consensus did not bring the judges closer to human annotators. We will release code, frozen rubrics, item identifiers, and judge scores.

This article explores how organizational applications of Artificial Intelligence (AI) impact digital leadership (DL) roles and the corresponding competencies and which approaches in Talent Management (TM) are needed to develop these. There is a gap in the literature regarding the dilemma faced by TM in filling talent pools for the key position of digital leaders, while competence requirements remain vague and distorted by the rapid changes driven by digital transformation. Based on a structured review of the current scientific literature, 72 cases from the European context, encompassing diverse industries and various corporate functions, are qualitatively analyzed to identify hurdles, success factors, and required behavior and subsequent competencies. The cases emphasize applying a step-by-step approach in organizations’ current digital transformation in the European context. Success factors highlight the importance of (digital) leaders equipped with manifold competencies. TM must broaden its scope when identifying leadership talent and become more inclusive. Individual learning journeys are a prerequisite for filling talent pools and, consequently, DL roles. This study represents the exploration into the implications for TM by analyzing DL and the requisite competences in AI applications within organizations. By capturing a current snapshot of DL, the study provides new insights into the necessary competencies and their implications for the future of TM.

This note shares a hypothesis based on my personal experience with ChatGPT over the last three months. I imagine there's already a lot of research out there, but my purpose is to show that we need more empirical data—either by gathering a wide range of user experiences or by seeing more single-case studies based on individual personal experiences. If some of my hypotheses aren't fully proven yet, I'd love for anyone to test them out based on their own personal experiences.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: This poster presents the research on the application of different approaches to the information extraction process and encoding of the 18th century Larramendi’s Trilingual Dictionary. The digitisation and computational analysis of historical dictionaries present significant challenges due to archaic typefaces, complex layouts, and inconsistent lexicographic structures. Manuel de Larramendi's Diccionario trilingüe castellano, bascuence y latin (1745, hereafter LAR), a foundational text for modern Basque lexicography, remained largely inaccessible in a structured digital format, available only as scanned facsimile images. Initial digitisation efforts employed a semi-automatic workflow combining machine learning (ML) for Optical Character Recognition (OCR) using Kraken and rule-based information extraction. The OCR for LAR was completed, and the resulting transcription was uploaded to Wikisource, a crowdsourcing platform that provides an interface for collaborative facsimile transcriptions. That process is ongoing and will very soon lead to an error-free digital version of the original text. Wikisource transcription quality is ensured by its rigorous, community-driven validation process, as completed works usually go through a two-step human review. The rule-based information extraction process facilitated the identification of Spanish headword candidates using positional data (line indentation) and orthographic features (capitalisation corresponding to alphabet sections). The extracted data was further enriched by linking Spanish lemmata to a contemporary reference, the Diccionario de Autoridades (1726-1739), and mapping historical Basque forms to modern standard lexicons. This work demonstrated the feasibility of converting a historical printed dictionary into structured datasets and linked data, though it highlighted limitations in fully capturing the complex microstructure of entries through rule-based methods alone (Lindemann & Alonso, 2021). The first approach to information extraction from LAR involved a hybrid methodology. For a more nuanced structural analysis, it was then employed the Elexifier toolchain, a ML-based application. A sample of dictionary columns was manually annotated with tags from the TEI-Lex0 schema and used for training a model to predict and segment lexicographic components—such as headwords, Basque and Latin equivalents—across the entire dictionary text. This ML approach proved complementary to the rule-based method, showing high precision for Spanish headwords and Basque translations but lower accuracy for Latin equivalents and cross-references, revealing the complexity of the dictionary’s microstructure. Advancing beyond specialised ML tools like Elexifier, contemporary research explores the application of general-purpose Large Language Models (LLMs) with vision capabilities for similar tasks. Inspired by methodologies applied to Estonian-German dictionaries (Jürviste & Jakobson, 2025) or to Swedish historical patent cards using the GPT-4o model (Xie et al., 2025), a third approach involves using DeepSeek, an advanced LLM, for the information extraction and encoding of LAR. The extraction of key microstructural elements like headwords (Spanish), translation equivalents (Basque, Latin), part-of-speech indicators, and example phrases and sentences is demanded from standard files, such as XML or JSON, or from the wikitext format text from Wikisource, with the few-shot prompting strategy, which basically consists of showing the model a few examples of inputs and desired outputs before asking it to solve the task. A fourth approach involves employing Microsoft Copilot, another multimodal LLM, for the same extraction task. The process consists of feeding Copilot with the same input and few-shot prompting, requesting structured TEI-Lex0 output that represents LAR’s tripartite entries. Following an experimental framework used for historical dictionaries (Jürviste & Jakobson, 2025), this allows for an evaluation of different model performances on identical material. Key evaluation metrics include the structural correctness of the generated markup (adherence to TEI-Lex0) and the model’s ability to correctly classify and relate the Spanish, Basque, and Latin lexical units within each entry. Preliminary analyses of the results suggest that DeepSeek encodes TEI-Lex0 schema with almost no syntax errors and can correct the dictionary’s microstructural inconsistencies in the encoded output file, whereas Microsoft Copilot tends to fail to follow consistently the encoding schema showed in the given examples. This comparative analysis extends the results of the mentioned studies about the strengths and weaknesses of different LLMs in handling the specific challenges posed by early modern bilingual/multilingual dictionary digitisation, particularly for languages with less digital representation. Nevertheless, it would be interesting for further digitisation processes to conduct experiments providing the tools with scanned images, because unlike the earlier workflow requiring separate OCR and segmentation stages, a vision-enabled LLM could potentially perform text recognition and semantic structuring in a single, integrated step. This approach promises a more direct path from facsimile to structured data, potentially reducing pipeline complexity and adapting more flexibly to layout irregularities. In conclusion, the initial work on LAR established a viable pipeline and valuable datasets from rule-based and specialised ML tools, although the evolution to general-purpose (vision-enabled) LLMs represents a significant shift in historical dictionary digitisation methodology. Approaches leveraging LLMs aim to integrate OCR, segmentation, and semantic encoding into a more efficient workflow. This research not only advances the digitisation of a key Basque lexicographic resource but also can contribute to computational historical lexicography by evaluating and refining modern AI-driven extraction techniques.

In the era of artificial intelligence (AI), sustainable education requires not only the integration of advanced technologies but also the cultivation of key competencies such as critical thinking. This study investigates English major students’ engagement with generative AI tools in translation learning, focusing on their usage patterns, critical thinking behaviors, and ethical awareness. A mixed-methods design combining questionnaire data and semi-structured interviews was employed to examine how students interact with AI in translation contexts. The results show that while students frequently use AI for translation, writing, and language learning, their engagement remains primarily functional and efficiency-driven. Although they display openness and flexibility toward AI, their reasoning confidence, self-regulation, and ethical reflection are underdeveloped, indicating surface-level interaction and overreliance on technological authority. These findings highlight the need to cultivate higher-order cognitive and ethical capacities in translation training. Central to this discussion is the conceptualization of the ideal learner in AI-assisted translation, a reflective, autonomous, and ethically aware individual who engages with AI as a partner in cognitive and moral development. Building on this, the study proposes pedagogical strategies that integrate AI literacy, process-oriented assessment, and teacher training to foster critical thinking and responsible AI use in sustainable translation education.

The article examines the semantic and contextual features of verbs expressing emotional states in English in literary discourse and the possibilities of their analysis using artificial intelligence. The study summarizes lexicon-based, machine learning, and hybrid approaches used in the automatic analysis of emotional lexicon, and evaluates the capabilities of modern NLP and AI models in detecting emotional units, semantic classification, frequency of processing, and determining contextual features. In literary texts, this concept is further expanded, because here the author's style, the characters’ speech, narrative strategies, and the reader’s interpretive activity interact with each other. The difficulties posed by ambiguity, metaphor, irony, and indirect emotional expression in literary discourse in automatic analysis are particularly emphasized. It is determined that although AI is an effective tool in the systematic analysis of emotional verbs, human verification of the results obtained from linguistic and philological perspectives is necessary. Expressing emotions through language is a pressing issue in modern linguistics. It has been established that in literary discourse, emotional meaning is formed not only by the semantics of individual words, but also by the interaction of narrative context, the character’s psychological state, and the author’s stylistic choices. Verbs expressing emotional states have been shown to play a significant role in representing the characters’ inner worlds and constructing the emotional-semantic structure of the text. The study shows that verbs expressing emotional states play an important role in shaping the internal state of characters and the emotional-semantic structure of the text in literary discourse. Since the meaning of these verbs depends on the context, the lexical-semantic approach in their analysis should be complemented by discursive and contextual analysis.

Background/Objectives: Adult-type diffuse gliomas (ADGs) are aggressive brain tumors with highly variable clinical outcomes. Prognostic assessment directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin (H&E)-stained whole-slide images (WSIs) could support personalized decision-making. Methods: To our knowledge, this is the first systematic benchmarking of pathology foundation models (FMs) and multiple instance learning (MIL) methods for overall survival (OS) risk stratification in ADGs under the 2021 World Health Organization (WHO) classification. A retrospective, multi-institutional cohort of 817 subjects from The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) was analyzed. Following tissue segmentation and patch-level curation, we evaluated 77 pathology FM-MIL combinations (11 FMs × 7 MIL methods), together with seven ResNet-50 baseline configurations (84 encoder-MIL configurations in total), using patient-level 10-fold cross-validation. A perturbation-based evaluation assessed attention mechanism faithfulness. Results: UNI2 paired with MambaMIL achieved the highest cross-validated concordance index (C-index = 0.77), whereas its time-dependent AUC was modest (0.60–0.61 at 12–36 months), and several combinations performed comparably. Kaplan–Meier analysis demonstrated significant separation between high- and low-risk groups (log-rank p = 9.16 × 10−17; hazard ratio [HR] = 2.90, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 2.23–3.76), with a median OS of 16.6 months (95% CI: 15.0–20.4) versus 63.5 months (95% CI: 43.9-NR), respectively. Tertile stratification confirmed a monotonic OS gradient from 94.5 months to 14.7 months (p = 3.25 × 10−17). Risk stratification within individual WHO 2021 types was not significant. Most domain-specific FMs outperformed the ImageNet-pretrained baseline, and the removal of highly attended patches reduced performance, supporting attention faithfulness. Conclusions: The AI-derived risk score remained associated with OS after adjustment for individual clinical and molecular variables, but independent prognostic value was not demonstrated in the fully adjusted model (HR = 1.32, 95% CI: 0.94–1.85, p = 0.104), and its discrimination largely reflects differences between WHO 2021 types. This benchmarking framework provides guidance for FM-MIL design in computational pathology applications targeting survival prediction; external validation is required before clinical application.
topics: Radiomics and Machine Learning in Medical Imaging

documents.abstract: The rapid growth of digital technologies has increased the number of cyberattacks targeting online systems and user data. Traditional security methods such as firewalls and intrusion detection systems are often unable to handle advanced and evolving threats effectively. To address this issue, this paper proposes an AI-Based Smart Honeypot System for Cyberattack Intelligence that combines machine learning, behavioral analysis, and deception techniques for detecting malicious activities in real time. The proposed system monitors user activities such as login attempts, typing behavior, session timing, and interaction patterns to identify suspicious behavior. A machine learning model is used to classify users as legitimate or malicious based on these behavioral features. If suspicious activity is detected, the user is redirected to a fake environment that appears similar to a real system, allowing the collection of attacker information without exposing sensitive data. The system was tested using simulated normal and malicious user activities, and the results showed improved detection accuracy with reduced false positives. The proposed approach not only improves cybersecurity protection but also helps in gathering valuable cyber threat intelligence for future analysis. Overall, the system provides a practical and scalable solution for modern cybersecurity challenges. Keywords: cybersecurity; artificial intelligence; machine learning; Anomaly detection; Intrusion Detection System; Smart Honeypot; Behavioral Analysis; Deception Technology; Threat Intelligence; Attack Detection

Purpose: This article examines the adequacy of international labour, human rights and trade-law frameworks for managing the digital labour transition driven by artificial intelligence, with attention to Universal Basic Income as a possible component of future social protection. Methodology: Using a qualitative documentary research design, the study analyses international legal instruments, International Labour Organization standards (ILOs), United Nations (UN) human rights frameworks and World Trade Organization (WTO) materials through a four-theme thematic coding structure. Results: International law provides important foundations for technological labour transition through rights to work, social security, non-discrimination and social dialogue, but does not establish Universal Basic Income as an international legal entitlement, while international trade rules facilitate technological diffusion without a comprehensive framework for distributing the social costs of displacement. Conclusions: The article argues for an integrated international framework linking artificial intelligence governance, labour-market transition, social protection, digital trade, skills development and sustainable fiscal mechanisms, while allowing states flexibility in determining whether Universal Basic Income should complement existing social security systems. Limitations: The study relies on documentary evidence rather than empirical labour-market data from affected workers, and rapidly evolving artificial intelligence capabilities mean exposure estimates may shift before policy frameworks are implemented. Contributions: The article offers a conceptual bridge linking labour law, human rights law, trade governance and fiscal policy around managing technological transition while protecting human dignity.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is changing the scope of decision support from model-assisted analysis toward systems in which algorithms, data, domain knowledge, and human judgment interact throughout the decision process [...]

This study presents an AI-driven approach to predicting marriage rates in Nigeria by analyzing the influence of socio-cultural and economic factors. Despite the central role marriage plays in Nigerian society, existing literature provides limited insight into how tradition, geopolitical zones, age, physical attractiveness, educational attainment, family background, and employment status collectively affect marital trends. This research applies supervised machine learning techniques— including logistic regression, decision trees, and random forest classifiers—to develop predictive models based on demographic data and survey responses. The analysis reveals that age, educational qualification, and employment status are the most significant predictors of marriage likelihood. Traditional norms and regional affiliations also contribute substantially, though their influence varies across Nigeria’s geopolitical zones. The study underscores the value of artificial intelligence in modeling complex social phenomena and offers a replicable methodological framework for social forecasting in diverse cultural settings. The findings have practical implications for policymakers, sociologists, and religious institutions seeking data-driven insights into marital behavior, and highlight the transformative potential of AI in interdisciplinary social research.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is being applied across textile-recycling systems to support material identification, automated sorting, process optimization, recovered-fiber assessment, sustainable composite design, and circular-economy decision-making. This systematic review synthesizes recent developments in AI-driven recycling pathways for sustainable textile composites. A structured Scopus search followed by predefined screening and eligibility assessment yielded 121 studies published between 2018 and 18 June 2026, and the review process was reported in accordance with the PRISMA 2020 framework. The reviewed evidence spans applications ranging from categorical fiber recognition to composition-aware and process-oriented approaches based on machine learning, deep learning, computer vision, spectroscopy, and optimization methods. Near-infrared, hyperspectral, Raman, and image-based systems have shown strong potential for identifying pure and blended textiles, while predictive models have been applied to estimate recovered-fiber quality, optimize recycling conditions, and predict mechanical and functional properties of recycled composites. Mechanical, chemical, and thermal recycling pathways exhibit different trade-offs in feedstock tolerance, material quality, process severity, and recovery potential, indicating that pathway selection remains context dependent. Life-cycle and circularity studies further suggest that higher recovery or recycled content does not necessarily correspond to lower environmental burden, particularly when energy use, substitution potential, material quality, and downstream recyclability are considered. Despite methodological advances, broader industrial implementation remains constrained by data representativeness, ground-truth quality, model transferability, explainability, and end-to-end system integration. Overall, the reviewed evidence suggests that further progress may depend on linking material characterization, quality-aware processing, composite-performance prediction, and sustainability assessment within interoperable and experimentally validated decision-support frameworks.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) is increasingly transforming assessment in higher education by enhancing Assessment for Learning (AfL) through personalized feedback, adaptive learning, and data-informed teaching. This chapter presents a systematic literature review examining how AI-driven assessment is reshaping teaching, learning, and assessment practices. Guided by the AfL framework, the review synthesizes current research on AI applications and their role in pedagogical transformation. Findings indicate that AI enables timely feedback, improves learner engagement, supports personalized learning experiences, and promotes authentic, process-oriented assessment. The review also highlights the increasing integration of AI into curriculum design and instructional decision-making. However, ethical concerns remain, including algorithmic bias, academic integrity, transparency, and data privacy. The chapter concludes that AI can strengthen formative assessment when implemented within sound pedagogical and ethical frameworks, supporting learner-centered transformation in higher education.

Mobility disabilities are among the most common disability types in the U.S., where the need to design safe powered mobility devices is increasingly important for user safety. For power wheelchair users, AI-enabled solutions have been introduced to avoid collisions. However, as control shifts from the user to automation, systems need to communicate intent clearly and maintain user trust. Auditory verbal cues can support decision-making: explanations may emphasize action-focused maneuvers or why-focused rationales. Tactile displays can also support communication through vibrations presented to the back or wrist. However, because safety-critical messages based on AI-inferred intent have not been systematically investigated and because power wheelchair users experience a different embodied interaction, there remains an opportunity to understand these factors. This pilot study explored the effects of communication strategy (action-focused, why-focused) and vibrotactile feedback location (seatback, wrist) on wheelchair performance and user perceptions. Six able-bodied participants completed wheelchair driving sessions while receiving obstacle alerts. Results indicated that seatback vibrations were associated with higher satisfaction ratings than wrist vibrations. No significant main effects were found for reaction time, decision-making accuracy, or usefulness ratings. These data can inform future studies designing intelligent wheelchair interfaces.
topics: Assistive Technology in Communication and Mobility

documents.abstract: This chapter critically examines the growing use of AI-mediated assessment in higher education and its implications for academic integrity, judgement, and institutional trust. While technologies such as automated grading, plagiarism detection, and remote proctoring are promoted for efficiency and consistency, their adoption represents a deeper sociotechnical shift that redistributes authority and reshapes accountability in assessment practices. Drawing on assessment theory, academic integrity scholarship, and algorithmic governance studies, the chapter argues that automation often reframes students as risks to be monitored rather than learners to be supported, raising concerns related to fairness and transparency. Rather than rejecting, the chapter advances a trust-centred framework emphasizing judgement, concluding that assessment quality cannot be secured through technological control.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The significance of mobile learning (m-learning) has been greatly highlighted by the advent of technology due to its flexibility, accessibility and capability of being used to learn at any time and place. The development of Large Language Models (LLMs) offers great potential for creating adaptive, conversational and content-aware learning experiences via mobile apps. Most existing mobile-learning systems, however, still provide largely static content and shallow personalisation, which limits sustained learner engagement and adaptive support. This paper presents the design and implementation of an Android-based, LLM-powered personalised m-learning platform that integrates four components: a conversational tutoring agent, an Item-Response-Theory (IRT)-based adaptive quiz engine, a Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) content-recommendation module, and an analytics-driven feedback loop. We describe the system architecture, the prompt-orchestration and knowledge-tracing pipelines, and a rigorous quasi-experimental evaluation protocol (pre-/post-test, System Usability Scale (SUS), and engagement analytics) designed for a controlled classroom deployment. To validate the core algorithmic contributions prior to human-subject trials, we conduct two simulation-based feasibility studies: (i) a synthetic-learner simulation comparing the adaptive difficulty engine against a static item sequence and (ii) a retrieval-precision benchmark comparing RAG-based content recommendation against keyword-matching on a synthetic tagged corpus. The adaptive engine delivered quiz items within the optimal challenge zone (0.4 < P(correct) < 0.8) for 77.8% of interactions, compared with 40.8% for the static baseline, while the RAG recommender achieved substantially higher retrieval precision at every cut-off (P@10 = 0.845 versus 0.483 for keyword matching). These results provide algorithmic evidence that the proposed adaptive and retrieval components behave as intended and motivate the full-scale classroom evaluation described in the protocol. The paper concludes with a discussion of design implications, limitations, and a concrete plan for the human-subject study and future extensions of the platform.
topics: Intelligent Tutoring Systems and Adaptive Learning

documents.abstract: The increasing integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) into English language education has introduced significant changes in teaching methodologies, learner engagement, assessment practices, and the development of linguistic competencies. AI-powered tools, including intelligent tutoring systems, generative language models, automated writing evaluation platforms, adaptive learning applications, speech-recognition technologies, and conversational agents, are creating opportunities for personalized instruction, immediate feedback, autonomous learning, and interactive language practice. However, their educational benefits are accompanied by substantial limitations and ethical concerns involving algorithmic bias, inaccurate linguistic feedback, data privacy, academic dishonesty, digital inequality, cultural representation, and excessive technological dependence. This study critically examines the opportunities, limitations, and ethical implications of AI-powered tools in English language education through a qualitative, literature-based analytical approach. Drawing upon contemporary scholarship, including research published in the Stanzaleaf International Journal of Multidisciplinary Studies, the paper explores how technological assistance can support linguistic development without compromising creativity, critical thinking, learner independence, or the responsibilities of educators. The study proposes a Human-Centred Ethical AI Integration Framework that integrates pedagogical relevance, learner autonomy, teacher mediation, digital equity, and ethical accountability. The analysis suggests that AI-assisted English language education is most defensible when technological systems enhance rather than replace human interaction, contextual understanding, and independent language production. The paper concludes that the sustainable integration of AI requires comprehensive digital literacy, transparent institutional policies, professional development, and learner-centred pedagogical practices.

Purpose Recent research has examined teachers' artificial intelligence (AI) competence, trust, and integration strategies, yet less is known about how AI-related work is coordinated through professional relationships. This study examines how AI-related collaboration is organized within professional learning community (PLC) infrastructure over time and how these relationships shape professional capital in practice. Design/methodology/approach A mixed methods case study was conducted in a Taiwanese junior high school engaged in national digital learning initiatives. The schoolwide PLC network provided organizational context, while two-wave AI Use and AI-integrated curriculum design (AI-ICD) networks among focal PLC educators were examined using descriptive network analyses and stochastic actor-oriented models. Interviews, observations, and organizational records were used to interpret the relational patterns. Findings AI-related collaboration showed two distinct but connected relational patterns. AI Use became more boundary-spanning, while AI-ICD remained concentrated within subject-aligned relationships. AI Use ties were positively associated with later AI-ICD ties, suggesting that exploration-oriented ties may have provided relational footholds for curriculum integration. Qualitative evidence showed how these arrangements shaped access to expertise, opportunities to develop AI-related pedagogical competence, and the exercise of professional judgment. It also identified time, readiness, perceived control, leadership recognition, and co-planning and verification routines as relevant conditions. Originality/value The study advances professional capital and network scholarship by showing how recurring AI-related demands are coordinated through existing PLC relationships and routines in distinct but connected relational forms. It contributes to the special issue by showing how relational arrangements shape access to expertise, pedagogical competence, and professional judgment under AI-related conditions.

Despite growing attention to artificial intelligence (AI) in organizational research, evidence on AI-related job insecurity and related technology-specific occupational threat perceptions remains fragmented. This systematic review synthesized associations with well-being impairment, maladaptive behavioral responses, and adaptive behavioral responses across 16 eligible studies, of which 11 contributed quantitative evidence. A tiered evidence strategy distinguished directly reported bivariate correlations used for primary synthesis from PLS-derived construct correlations and other model-dependent evidence retained for extended exploratory analyses. Five independent primary estimates showed a positive average association with well-being impairment, r = 0.317, 95% CI [0.084, 0.518], I2 = 97.35%. Six independent bivariate correlations showed a positive average association with maladaptive behavioral responses, r = 0.215, 95% CI [0.101, 0.324], I2 = 82.43%. Only two independent primary estimates were available for adaptive responses, precluding a primary pooled estimate; an extended exploratory synthesis remained small and statistically uncertain, r = 0.044, 95% CI [−0.020, 0.107]. AI-related occupational threat perceptions were more consistently associated with well-being impairment and maladaptive responses than with adaptation in the available literature. Substantial heterogeneity indicates considerable variation across settings and limit interpretation of these average associations as uniform effects.

This research project aims to improve adherence to a Dutch digital self-help program designed to support individuals in reducing or stopping alcohol consumption. Digital self-help interventions are increasingly recognized as accessible and cost-effective preventive tools that prevent people going seek for help at traditional addiction care. However, their effectiveness is strongly dependent on sustained user engagement. Within the current Jellinek Alcohol Self-help program, approximately 2,200 individuals create an account annually, yet only about 20% progress to the third phase of the intervention, indicating substantial dropout and limited adherence. The central objective of this study is to enhance adherence by introducing a conversational agent (CA) that provides personalized, motivational, and informational support throughout the intervention. The CA leverage a large language model (LLM) to generate tailored messages and is designed to simulate supportive guidance, without replacing professional treatment. Its use is optional and it does not serve a therapeutic or diagnostic function. In addition to the CA, AI-driven personalized reminder messages will be sent to participants throughout the intervention to encourage continued engagement with the program. This adaptation of the intervention is a responds to previously identified user needs, including a desire for more personalization, feedback on progress (e.g., alcohol registration), and motivating reminders comparable to those used in digital learning platforms. Participants who enroll in the Jellinek Alcohol Self-help program and meet the predefined inclusion criteria, including be adult (18 years or older), an AUDIT score ≤20, no current treatment for alcohol-related problems, no pregnancy or breastfeeding, and no reported suicidal ideation during screening will be asked to participate in research. After providing informed consent, participants complete baseline assessments of alcohol use, substance use, psychological distress, and quality of life. Follow-up assessments are conducted four weeks after the start of the intervention and twelve weeks after baseline. The study uses a non-randomized sequential A/B design. Participants who enroll during the first half of the study period receive the standard self-help intervention, whereas those enrolling during the second half receive an AI-enhanced version that includes a conversational agent and AI-driven personalized reminder messages. The primary outcome is adherence to the intervention, assessed using platform-based usage data, including the number of completed modules and exercises, time spent using the intervention, and number of logins. Secondary outcomes include alcohol consumption and alcohol-related problems, other substance use, psychological distress, quality of life, and program usability/satisfaction. Fort the participants who could use the conversational agent, additional questionnaires about the acceptibility, feasibility and usability of the conversational agents will be asked. These outcomes are measured using validated instruments, including the TLFB, AUDIT, MATE, DASS, MANSA, SUS, AIM, IAM, FIM, CUQ and CSQ. This study aims to evaluate whether the addition of a conversational agent and AI-driven personalized reminder messages is associated with improved adherence to the Jellinek Alcohol Self-help program. In addition, the study will examine whether participants using the AI-enhanced version of the intervention show different outcomes in alcohol use, psychological distress, quality of life, and program usability compared with participants using the standard version of the program. The findings will provide insight into the potential added value of AI-supported features within digital alcohol interventions and inform the further development and optimization of the Jellinek Alcohol Self-help program. If the AI-enhanced version is associated with higher adherence, this may indicate that conversational support and personalized reminders can help users remain engaged with online self-help interventions for a longer period of time.

The reciprocal relationship between large language models (LLMs) and knowledge graphs (KGs) opens new opportunities for knowledge discovery from scientific literature; however, most approaches address only one direction of this interaction. In complex biomedical domains, ensuring reliability, interpretability, and traceability remains challenging, making expert supervision essential. In this work, we propose a framework that integrates LLMs, KGs, and a Human-in-the-Loop scheme for constructing, evaluating, and reasoning over Evidence-based Knowledge Graphs (E-KGs), explicitly linking each extracted triplet to supporting textual evidence, and demonstrate its application to study the phenomenon of resistance in ovarian cancer. The E-KG was constructed using MedGemma-27B, with experts participating throughout the E-KG lifecycle, supported by our interactive visualization tools. We evaluated the E-KG through an expert-driven protocol assessing coherence and biological plausibility with inter-annotator agreement (Gwet’s AC1 coefficient), complemented by GraphRAG-based tasks, including link prediction (Hits@k, MRR) and a question-answering case study (faithfulness and answer relevance by LLM-as-a-judge and expert audit). The framework produced a coherent, plausible, and auditable E-KG, highlighting the potential of evidence-grounded knowledge to support LLM-based reasoning. To our knowledge, we introduce the first E-KG specialized in ovarian cancer resistance, providing an expert-validated resource that advances trustworthy and explainable AI for biomedical knowledge discovery.

topics: Physical Unclonable Functions (PUFs) and Hardware Security

documents.abstract: This study considers the cognitive factors influencing the adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) coding agents among software engineers in Agile development environments. In this context, Transparency refers to the degree to which an AI system’s decision processes are clear or understandable to its users, while Trust denotes the confidence developers place in the reliability and correctness of AI-generated code. Specifically, it analyzes the roles of Transparency and Trust as predictors of developers’ Behavioral Intention to deploy AI-generated code. Using a quantitative, cross-sectional survey design administered to 19 Agile software professionals, this study uses descriptive statistics, Pearson correlation analysis, and simple and multiple linear regression to test a mediation model based on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM). In this exploratory pilot sample, Trust emerged as the strongest predictor of Behavioral Intention (β = 0.64, p = 0.007), though findings should be interpreted cautiously given the limited sample size. Trust demonstrated the strongest association with Behavioral Intention, while Transparency showed a non-significant positive association with Trust. The observed pattern is consistent with a possible indirect relationship, although mediation was not confirmed in this sample. This evidence suggests that organizations seeking to improve AI adoption in development teams should prioritize the reliability and accuracy of AI tools, conditions that encourage trust, over transparency features alone. This study adds to the cognitive engineering literature on human–AI interaction in high-cognitive-demand work environments.

With 60 years of research, knowledge-based system has travelled a long journey from early small-scale rule-based programs to modern super-large-scale knowledge graphs. Several multithreading technical stages can be broadly categorized: early history of rule-based system, knowledge engineering, semantic network, semantic web, ontology engineering, knowledge graph, and recent advances driven by machine learning. In the past couple years, the whole area of artificial intelligence including knowledge-based system has been significantly influenced by large language models, which dramatically increases the understanding and utilization of knowledge by increasing to an extremely large scale. Considering the long-standing intrinsic problems of large language models such as hallucination and lack of explainability, the challenge of how to build reliable large-scale knowledge-based systems in an effective and economical way still exists. From the overview of the developing history, we can see a promising research direction of combining large language models with those traditional knowledge-based frameworks.

The development of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in higher education has provided students with new opportunities to facilitate academic writing, including thesis preparation. However, AI use also raises concerns regarding student independence and their beliefs about control over academic outcomes (Locus of Control). This study aims to describe the levels of AI use, independence, and Locus of Control among students in the Building Engineering Education program at Universitas Negeri Malang during thesis preparation. A quantitative descriptive approach was employed, involving 93 students currently writing their theses. Data were collected using a Likert-scale questionnaire and analyzed descriptively to identify the tendencies of each variable. The results indicate that AI use falls into the high category, with a mean score of 63.53. Meanwhile, student independence falls into the moderate category, with a mean score of 33.27. Locus of Control is also in the moderate category, with a mean score of 26.53, although students demonstrate a predominantly internal orientation. These findings suggest that students utilize AI as an academic support tool while maintaining independence and confidence in their own abilities to complete their theses. Therefore, AI use should be accompanied by critical thinking, independent decision-making, and academic responsibility to ensure that technology supports the thesis-writing process without replacing students' active involvement.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: This study examines Technology Education Students Perceptions of ChatGPT use in distance learning, focusing on its benefits, ease of use, and risks. The study employs a descriptive quantitive approach. The participants are Technology Education students who have experience using ChatGPT for learning activities. Data are collected through a five-point Likert-scale questionnaire covering indicators of benefits, ease of use, and risks. The data are analyzed using descriptive statistics in the form of the percentages and mean scores. This study is expected to provide an overview of students perceptions of ChatGPT as a learning- support technology and the considerations involved in its responsible use. The findings are expected to contribute to strengthening AI literacy and the appropriate use of generative artificial intelligence in Technology Education learning.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The ability of Large Language Models (LLMs) to outperform humans on many intellectual tasks has created a difficult landscape for assessing student work. One strategy is designing assignments to be specifically difficult for AI. However, LLMs have been shown to perform well on general chemistry problems across topics, and new models continue to make AI-proofing assignments more difficult. In this work, we evaluate the recently released GPT-5 Thinking model across a set of 1736 questions from the Openstax general chemistry textbook. While GPT-5 achieves near-perfect accuracy overall, categorizing questions by the types of cognitive skills required elucidates specific weaknesses. Notably, GPT-5 tends to make major errors when asked to create figures. These findings inform best practices for AI-resistant assignment design.
