documents.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI), robotics, computer vision, Internet of Things (IoT), satellite navigation, remote sensing, and autonomous control systems is transforming the design and operation of modern agricultural machinery. Agricultural machinery is increasingly evolving from conventional mechanical equipment into intelligent cyber-physical systems capable of sensing field conditions, processing large volumes of data, making operational decisions, and executing agricultural tasks with limited human intervention. This article examines the application of artificial intelligence and automation technologies in tractors, harvesters, sprayers, robotic platforms, unmanned aerial vehicles, and other agricultural machinery. The study is based on a systematic analysis of scientific publications, international institutional reports, and documented agricultural technology adoption data. Particular attention is given to autonomous navigation, machine vision, precision spraying, variable-rate application, crop monitoring, yield prediction, robotic weeding, harvesting, and safety systems. Evidence from the United States demonstrates substantial growth in precision-agriculture adoption: automated guidance systems were used on more than half of the acreage planted to several major crops, while in 2023 guidance autosteering was used by 52 percent of midsize farms and 70 percent of large-scale crop-producing farms. Scientific literature also demonstrates the growing role of machine learning in yield estimation, nitrogen management, disease detection, and robotic perception. However, high acquisition costs, inadequate rural connectivity, data governance issues, cybersecurity, technical complexity, and safety risks remain significant barriers. The study concludes that AI-enabled agricultural machinery can contribute to higher operational efficiency, more precise input application, reduced operator fatigue, improved resource management, and greater agricultural sustainability, provided that technological development is accompanied by appropriate infrastructure, human-capacity development, interoperability standards, and safety regulation.

This article examines whether artificial intelligence can genuinely participate in practices of care within healthcare settings and what implications this development has for healthcare chaplaincy. Drawing on recent research on artificial empathy, the paper argues that AI can support caregiving practices instrumentally but cannot replace the interpersonal and relational dimensions constitutive of authentic care. The analysis introduces the concept of cognitive safety as a framework for evaluating AI-mediated interactions in contexts of vulnerability. Particular attention is given to empathy, responsibility, practical wisdom, and relational presence as dimensions that remain irreducibly human. The article concludes that chaplaincy should adopt a model of balanced integration in which AI serves as a supportive tool while preserving the centrality of human encounter, spiritual accompaniment, and moral agency.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is poised to reshape operations across industries. Yet its real-world impact reveals a jagged and uneven implementation frontier. To make sense of this emerging landscape, we develop a foundational framework that synthesizes research and practice at the intersection of AI and Operations Management (OM), anchored in three interdependent pillars: (1) AI for OM, (2) OM for AI, and (3) Human–AI Interaction. First, AI for OM analyzes how AI enhances core operational processes, including design, procurement, production, and delivery. Second, OM for AI argues that scaling AI safely and effectively stands to benefit from core OM principles, including workflow design, capacity management, process control, drift detection, and continuous improvement, all of which are central to AI development and deployment. Third, Human–AI Interaction emphasizes the role of trust, incentives, and organizational design in mediating how humans and machines learn from and collaborate with each other. This triadic framework provides a foundation for organizing research on AI and OM and offers practical guidance for integrating AI into business and societal systems.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly presented as a transformative tool for addressing longstanding governance challenges, including bureaucratic inefficiency, corruption, poor transparency and weak citizen responsiveness. Yet whether AI can genuinely serve as a panacea for these challenges within a large, institutionally complex federation such as Nigeria remains an open empirical question. This study examined artificial intelligence and public service delivery as a panacea for global governance challenges, drawing on the Nigerian experience. Anchored on New Public Management (NPM) Theory and Digital Era Governance (DEG) Theory, the study adopted a descriptive survey design. A population of six hundred (600) public servants was drawn from five (5) selected federal public service institutions and the Federal Inland Revenue Service (FIRS), the National Identity Management Commission (NIMC), the Nigeria Immigration Service (NIS), the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) and the Corporate Affairs Commission (CAC) spanning offices across Nigeria's six geo-political zones, out of which five hundred and fifty (550) copies of a structured questionnaire were administered and five hundred and thirty (530) were completed, returned and found usable, representing a 96.4 per cent response rate. Data were analysed using mean, standard deviation and chi-square statistics. Findings show that the extent of AI adoption in Nigerian public service delivery was moderate, concentrated mainly in digital communication, records management and citizen-facing chatbot platforms, with more advanced predictive-analytics and automated-decision applications far less diffused. AI adoption was found to have a significant positive effect on the efficiency of public service delivery and a significant positive effect on addressing global governance challenges such as transparency, accountability and responsiveness in the Nigerian public service. The study concludes that while artificial intelligence cannot on its own resolve Nigeria's governance challenges, it represents a substantial enabling tool that, when combined with institutional reform, adequate infrastructure and human-capacity development, can meaningfully strengthen public service delivery and governance outcomes. It is recommended that the Federal Government sustain and scale existing AI-in-governance initiatives, invest in civil service AI literacy and establish clear regulatory standards for AI use in public institutions.

Small and medium enterprises (SMEs) are the driving force of developing economies, yet they remain limited in resources to implement artificial intelligence (AI), and there is little empirical evidence that AI adoption is associated with small business growth in the region, particularly in Central Asia. This research makes two contributions. First, we propose a concise framework that links classes of AI technologies to SME competitiveness features and identifies machine learning, natural language processing, and generative AI as low-cost, quick-return priority areas for resource-constrained firms. Second, using 16 years of data (2010–2025) for the Bukhara region of Uzbekistan, we estimate ARIMA models for each indicator and forecast eight small business indicators to 2030. Small business output is projected to grow at a steady rate of approximately 16% by 2030, with digital adoption and preferential credit support emerging as indicators associated with long-run growth. Forecast accuracy is high for the human-capital indicator and acceptable for output. The evidence is associational rather than causal: the framework and the forecasts converge on a single, cautiously formulated proposition—the adoption of low-cost AI is measurably associated with the sustainable competitiveness of SMEs, providing a practical, evidence-based starting point for regional AI policy in developing countries.
topics: Impact of AI and Big Data on Business and Society

documents.abstract: In recent years, the rise of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has not only transformed industry, communication, and healthcare, but has also entered the domain of religion raising profound questions about the nature of the sacred and divine mediation. This article investigates the sociological implications of AI in religious settings, focusing on how believers and institutions negotiate the role of intelligent machines in facilitating spiritual encounters. Drawing on Emile Durkheim’s notion of the sacred and profane, Peter Berger’s sacred canopy, and posthumanist thought, the study is grounded in a qualitative, sociological approach. Data were drawn from secondary sources and illustrative case studies in Nigeria’s Christian, Islamic, and African Traditional Religious (ATR) contexts. It explores how AI-powered preachers, prayer bots, and algorithmic devotionals are disrupting traditional models of religious authority and divine communication. The article argues that while AI may democratise access to spiritual resources, it also provokes anxiety about the loss of sacred intimacy and the mechanisation of faith. It concludes by calling for interdisciplinary collaboration between Religious Studies, Sociology, and AI ethics to critically assess the future of the sacred in an age of machine agency.
topics: Religion and Sociopolitical Dynamics in Nigeria

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence and the Transformation of College Libraries in India: Applications, Readiness, Challenges and a Framework for Responsible Adoption Dr. Amar Nath* Artificial intelligence (AI) is reshaping academic information environments by extending conventional library automation towards intelligent discovery, conversational assistance, metadata support, recommendation, research assistance, multilingual access and data-informed service planning. This paper examines the implications of AI for Indian college libraries, with particular attention to services, infrastructure, professional competencies, research support, accessibility, ethics and institutional readiness. A qualitative narrative review and conceptual analysis are employed, drawing on scholarly literature, Indian empirical studies, national policy documents and professional guidance. The review indicates that AI can augment routine library work and create more responsive, inclusive and research-oriented services, but its value depends on data quality, connectivity, interoperability, staff capabilities, privacy safeguards, copyright compliance and human oversight. The paper distinguishes AI-enabled functions from conventional digital automation and cautions against treating all technology-based library services as AI. A six-stage implementation framework—Assess, Prepare, Pilot, Integrate, Evaluate and Scale—is proposed for Indian colleges. The study argues that responsible AI adoption should be problem-led rather than technology-led and should strengthen, rather than displace, professional librarianship. The future-ready college library is therefore conceptualised as a human-centred intelligent knowledge ecosystem in which AI supports discovery, learning and research while librarians retain responsibility for judgement, context, ethics and information literacy. *Post Graduate Government College, Sector-11, Chandigarh, India, Affiliated to Panjab University, Chandigarh Email: sharmago4amar@gmail.com

documents.abstract: Background. The rapid development of digital dentistry and artificial intelligence (AI) is expanding the range of technologies available for diagnosis, treatment planning, prosthetic design, and outcome prediction. Material selection remains a clinically important component of prosthodontic treatment because the choice of restorative material must account for mechanical, functional, biological, and esthetic requirements. Aim. To analyze recent literature on the application of AI in prosthodontics, with particular attention to its potential role in supporting restorative material selection, integrating clinical and digital parameters, predicting prosthetic outcomes, and personalizing treatment planning. Materials and methods. A narrative analytical review was developed from literature published during seven completed calendar years (January 2019–December 2025). Relevant publications were identified in PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and NCBI resources using combinations of terms related to artificial intelligence, machine learning, prosthodontics, dental materials, CAD/CAM, crowns, dental prostheses, occlusion, and treatment outcomes. Publications were thematically analyzed according to AI application, type of prosthodontic task, data source, clinical purpose, reported outcomes, and limitations. Results. The reviewed literature demonstrates that AI is increasingly applied in prosthodontic diagnostics, treatment planning, automated crown design, finish-line detection, occlusal assessment, prediction of prosthetic outcomes, and digital workflows. AI-assisted CAD systems have shown potential to improve design efficiency and, in selected studies, achieve clinically acceptable crown fit. However, the evidence remains heterogeneous with substantial differences in datasets, algorithms, validation procedures, and outcome measures. Direct evidence supporting independently validated AI systems for individualized restorative material selection remains limited. Current evidence therefore supports the use of AI primarily as a clinical decision-support tool rather than as an autonomous system for material selection. Conclusions. AI has considerable potential to support individualized material selection and prosthodontic treatment planning by integrating multiple clinical and digital parameters. At the same time, current evidence does not support treating AI as an autonomous replacement for professional clinical judgment. Direct validation of AI systems specifically designed to select restorative materials remains limited, and many predictive models require stronger external validation and prospective clinical evaluation. The most appropriate current framework is therefore a human-in-the-loop decision-support model in which AI augments, rather than replaces, clinical expertise

documents.abstract: This theoretical paper presents a conceptual framework for understanding the integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learning contexts. Drawing on established foreign language acquisition theories, sociocultural learning paradigms, and emerging digital pedagogy scholarship, the paper develops the AI-Enhanced Foreign Language Learning (AEFLL) framework around a specific theoretical proposition. AI tools, unlike the human interlocutors around which classical SLA theory was built, can decouple the cognitive, affective, and social functions that face-to-face instruction has traditionally delivered as a single, integrated package. This decoupling, rather than the broader observation that cognition, affect, and social interaction all matter for language learning, constitutes the framework’s central theoretical contribution. It generates directional, testable hypotheses about how different AI tools, by recombining these functions in different proportions, produce different developmental trade-offs for EFL learners. The paper situates this argument within current scholarship on human-AI collaboration, critical AI literacy, and the sociopolitical risks of AI-mediated education, including linguistic inequality and data colonialism, and offers a balanced account of the psychological benefits and risks associated with AI-mediated learning. Practical implications for curriculum design and teacher professional development are discussed alongside a structured agenda for empirical validation.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) and Machine Learning (ML) are changing Library and Information Science (LIS) by impacting on user services, cataloguing, and information retrieval; however, the literature on how this is happening has not been systematically catalogued. To fill this gap, this study was conducted using a bibliometric analysis of the papers pertaining to AI, ML and LIS published from 2015 to 2024. The aim of the study is to analyse the growth of publication, citation trends, characteristics of authors, keyword co-occurrence networks, and international collaboration in this field to discover the intellectual structures and future trends of the field. A total of 2180 documents from 436 sources were retrieved by applying a structured keyword search strategy, after removing the duplicates and the irrelevant documents, the retrieved documents were analysed with the help of the Bibliometrix package in RStudio and VOSviewer for descriptive bibliometric analysis and network-based bibliometric analysis respectively. Results indicate an increase at an annual rate of 43.16%, with only 2024 reporting 707 publications or 32.43% of the total. The data set contained 7,623 authors, each of whom authored an average of 3.84 co-authors per document, and only 71 documents (3.26%) had a single author, showing a very collaborative research culture. The most common and most cited author keywords were “machine learning” (7,633 citations), “deep learning” (4,182), and “learning systems” (3,272). The document with the most citations garnered 351 citations, with India becoming the top among the contributing countries and the largest node in the international co-authorship networks. From these results, it can be inferred that AI/ML research in LIS is growing rapidly, is collaborative in nature and has a higher focus on machine learning and deep learning applications. Based on the study, the researcher concludes that this bibliometric mapping will be a baseline reference for researchers, librarians and policy makers to understand the evolution of AI and ML in LIS and to identify emerging research areas like generative AI, explainable AI and intelligent digital libraries.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming modern marketing by integrating predictive analytics with generative creativity to enhance personalization, efficiency, and strategic decision-making. Predictive models enable data-driven insights through customer segmentation, demand forecasting, churn analysis, and campaign optimization, while generative AI introduces scalable content creation, automated design, and innovative product prototyping. Together, these technologies create intelligent marketing ecosystems capable of delivering real-time, context-aware experiences across diverse channels. However, challenges related to data quality, algorithmic bias, ethical concerns, privacy regulations, and system integration must be addressed to ensure responsible adoption. This chapter explores foundational AI techniques, key applications, creative advancements, and emerging research directions that shape the future of AI-driven marketing, emphasizing the need for transparent, ethical, and human-centric innovation.

The rapid advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) has transformed the foundations of modern marketing, shifting from data-driven decision-making toward an era of intelligent creativity that fuses predictive analytics with generative innovation. This chapter conceptually examines how the integration of predictive and generative AI—through the Integrated Predictive–Generative Framework (IPGF)—redefines marketing intelligence by merging analytical precision with creative synthesis. Through theoretical analysis and case-based interpretation, the chapter explores predictive AI in forecasting consumer behavior and generative AI in producing personalized, emotionally resonant content. It also identifies ethical, psychological, and social implications associated with AI-driven creativity, emphasizing transparency, fairness, and human oversight as essential principles for sustainable, human-centered marketing ecosystems.

Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming medical education and clinical practice, requiring digital, critical, and ethical competencies. This study aimed to assess medical students’ attitudes toward AI, including perceived benefits, risks, and use in medical training. Methods: A mixed-methods, descriptive study used an electronic questionnaire comprising sociodemographic data and 13 items adapted from the authorized Artificial Intelligence Attitude Scale. Responses were recorded on a five-point Likert scale, with reverse-coding of negative items. Total and subscale scores for benefits, risks/threats, and use were calculated. Participants were medical students from the 1st to 6th years at the School of Medicine of Jundiaí (FMJ). Results: Among 436 students, attitudes toward AI were generally favorable. No significant gender difference was observed (p = 0.291), whereas scores differed significantly across training years (p = 0.025), with higher scores among advanced students. Despite recognizing AI’s benefits, students reported concerns regarding reliability, clinical autonomy, ethical implications, and gaps in practical knowledge. Conclusions: AI is positively perceived by medical students, particularly those in advanced years. These findings support structured AI integration into medical curricula to promote critical, ethical, and responsible use in medical education and future clinical practice.

documents.abstract: Ocular surface malignancies include ocular surface squamous neoplasia (OSSN), con-junctival melanoma, and conjunctival lymphoma. These rare disorders may threaten vi-sion and, in some cases, life. Early identification may be difficult because malignant le-sions can resemble benign ocular surface conditions. Artificial intelligence (AI), including machine learning and deep learning, has emerged as a potential aid to detection, classi-fication, and referral. This structured narrative review, organized with reference to SANRA principles, synthesizes PubMed/MEDLINE literature on AI applications in ocular surface oncology available through 29 August 2026. We examine slit-lamp photography, anterior segment optical coherence tomography, in vivo confocal microscopy, ultrasound biomicroscopy, and smartphone imaging. Deep-learning models have shown promising performance in selected binary OSSN tasks, whereas multiclass studies report lower sen-sitivity for rare malignancies such as conjunctival melanoma and lymphoma. Smartphone-based screening has also been evaluated in a prospective referral pathway, although the reference standard and verification process limit interpretation of popula-tion-level sensitivity. Dataset imbalance, image-acquisition variability, limited external and prospective validation, explainability, and workflow integration remain barriers to implementation. Future work should prioritize multicenter datasets, standardized acquisition, calibrated thresholds, and prospective human–AI evaluations. Current evidence supports further evaluation of AI as an adjunct for detection and referral, not as a re-placement for specialist assessment or histopathology.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming pharmacy practice by supporting medication management, clinical decision-making, patient education, and pharmacy operations. Although AI research in the Middle East has expanded rapidly, the evidence remains fragmented across countries, technologies, and practice settings. This scoping review aimed to systematically map the current evidence on AI applications, adoption, perceived benefits, implementation barriers, and ethical and regulatory considerations in pharmacy practice across the Middle East. Methods A scoping review was conducted according to the Joanna Briggs Institute methodology and reported following the PRISMA-ScR guidelines. PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science were systematically searched for English-language studies investigating AI in pharmacy practice in Middle Eastern countries. Two reviewers independently screened studies and extracted data. Findings were synthesized narratively according to AI applications, utilization, pharmacists' awareness and attitudes, perceived benefits, implementation barriers, ethical and regulatory issues, and future research priorities. Results A total of 15 studies published between 2023 and 2026, involving 8,117 participants across multiple Middle Eastern countries, were included. Most studies were cross-sectional surveys (93.3%) evaluating pharmacists' awareness, perceptions, and readiness to adopt AI. ChatGPT and large language models were the most frequently investigated technologies, primarily supporting medication information, patient counselling, medication management, and clinical decision support, while AI-enabled robotics focused on dispensing and pharmacy operations. Pharmacists generally demonstrated high awareness and positive attitudes toward AI, and some studies reported previous or individual use; however, evidence of routine use and organization-level implementation remained limited. Perceived benefits included improved clinical decision-making, medication safety, and workflow efficiency, whereas major barriers included inadequate AI training, limited technological infrastructure, implementation costs, organizational readiness, and concerns regarding privacy, cybersecurity, algorithmic bias, transparency, and professional accountability. Conclusion AI has considerable potential to enhance pharmacy practice across the Middle East, but implementation remains at an early stage, with the available literature predominantly reflecting pharmacists' perceptions of anticipated benefits rather than evidence of demonstrated clinical effectiveness. Strengthening AI education, digital infrastructure, governance frameworks, and implementation research will be essential to support the safe, ethical, and evidence-based integration of AI into pharmacy practice.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: PURPOSE: To assess the performance of artificial intelligence (AI) compared with physicians in detecting rotator cuff tear (RCT) on medical imaging and evaluating the ability of AI to predict outcomes after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair. METHODS: A comprehensive search was conducted in the PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases from their inception to July 15, 2025. The criteria were as follows: (1) original studies employing AI to detect RCT or predict outcomes after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair and (2) case reports, reviews, and editorials were excluded. This review followed the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses guidelines and was registered on the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews. RESULTS: A total of 37 studies met the inclusion and exclusion criteria, encompassing 46,593 patients. The mean age of the patients was 55.8 years, with an average female representation of 52.2%. AI models developed for diagnosing RCT using magnetic resonance imaging, ultrasound, and radiographic images showed excellent performance, achieving average area under the curves and accuracies of 89.5% and 0.93, 91% and 0.97, and 84% and 0.86, respectively. AI models using radiographs and magnetic resonance imaging have shown performance in diagnosing RCT that surpasses that of junior clinicians, with magnetic resonance imaging-based models performing at a level comparable to senior clinicians. AI models developed to predict retear after arthroscopic rotator cuff repair showed an average accuracy of 83.4% and an area under the curve of 0.83. Older and women were the most common risk factors for postoperative retear identified in the included studies. CONCLUSIONS: AI models significantly improved diagnostic accuracy based on medical imaging and showed promising predictive performance, particularly regarding rotator cuff retear. However, predictions related to functional scores exhibited relatively lower accuracy. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, systematic review of Level II and III studies.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: The metaverse connects immersive interfaces, virtual environments, artificial intelligence, extended reality, cloud and edge computing, digital twins, communication networks, and blockchain-based services. These technologies can support education, entertainment, commerce, training, and digital ownership, but they also create a broad, evolving cybersecurity surface. Identity theft, privacy loss, abnormal network activity, deepfake-based impersonation, and digital-asset fraud can occur across interconnected layers. This paper presents an independently written, student-oriented study of AI-assisted cybersecurity for the metaverse. It focuses on intelligent authentication, AI-based intrusion detection, privacy-aware learning, and protection of blockchain and NFT ecosystems. The paper describes a layered framework in which relevant security data are collected, processed with suitable AI methods, converted into risk decisions, and followed by proportionate responses. The study also discusses data quality, latency, interoperability, privacy, model attacks, and the need for human oversight. The central view is that AI should complement established cybersecurity controls rather than replace them.

This chapter critically examines AI-supported assessment as a transformative yet ethically complex development in higher education. It frames AI-mediated assessment as a socio-pedagogical practice shaped by equity, integrity, and curriculum governance. While tools such as automated grading, learning analytics, and generative feedback can enhance formative assessment, constructive alignment, and inclusion, they also pose risks of bias, surveillance, opacity, automation bias, and weakened professional judgment—especially in resource-constrained and Global South contexts. Drawing on inclusive education, assessment-for-learning, and human-centered AI frameworks, the chapter proposes a layered ecosystem model for responsible implementation. It argues that AI can strengthen quality and trust only when embedded in transparent, ethically governed, and pedagogically grounded systems that uphold human dignity and educational justice.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI), particularly Generative AI (GenAI) and Large Language Models (LLMs), is reshaping digital services while raising ethical, legal, cybersecurity, privacy, and alignment challenges. This narrative review provides an interdisciplinary synthesis of these challenges, examining GenAI-related risks, the evolving European Union regulatory landscape, including the AI Act, cybersecurity threats to AI systems, and core principles for trustworthy AI. Beyond this synthesis, the paper’s central contribution is a reconceptualisation of the privacy paradox: where data collection is structurally entrenched, non-participation is costly, and viable lower-data alternatives are lacking, the gap between privacy attitudes and disclosure behaviour can reflect structural constraints on participation as well as individual decisions, a conditional account we term “digital inevitability” (DIGINEV). GenAI does not create this condition but can intensify it by inferring sensitive information from indirect signals. We develop this into a conceptual framework that proposes how constraints on participation may interact with user resignation and identifies possible responses through regulation, design, collective action, and viable alternatives. The paper further discusses AI alignment as a supporting consideration in the governance of GenAI systems. The findings offer an integrated perspective for future research, regulatory development, and responsible AI deployment, anchored in the DIGINEV framework.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT Artificial intelligence (AI) is dramatically changing the healthcare landscape by providing patients, clinicians, administrators, and public health professionals with tools aiming to improve efficiency, outcomes, and experience in health. As elsewhere, New York State (NYS) experiences high demand for - and high investment in - transformation in healthcare with AI tools, though little is known about clinicians’ use and interest in adopting AI tools in their work. A large share of the nation’s future primary care clinicians train and work in NYS, and the state’s ability to establish clear policies, provide tools, and elevate AI competency have implications for care delivery nationally. As a result, we undertook this analysis of NYS clinicians’ use of AI to better understand opportunities for its adoption and inclusion in continuing education. For this analysis, we included healthcare providers who deliver ambulatory or specialty medical care within NYS, with use/frequency/purpose of AI tools by clinicians in their work as the main outcome. Of 305 NYS clinical providers responding, 23.4% indicated they use AI tools for work, and 11.1% report monthly use, 8.5% weekly use, and 4.6% daily use. AI was primarily used to search guidelines and ask clinical questions, followed by identifying drug interactions, analyzing data, analyzing images/labs, and creating care plans and patient recommendations. AI use did not vary significantly across professional disciplines or practice types, though independent practitioners were significantly more likely than advanced practice providers to use AI in their work, as were providers using social media and digital methods for obtaining continuing education. AI use increased substantially in 2025 compared with 2024. Overall, our findings suggest that programs targeting clinicians could incorporate these findings in designing accessible and acceptable AI-related continuing education opportunities to help familiarize clinicians with opportunities and risks for integrating AI tools into their practices. Author Summary AI tools are rapidly gaining traction in the delivery of healthcare. We found that clinician use of AI was quite limited (23%), though growing. Those using AI tools used them sparingly in their work, with only about 5% reporting daily use. The purposes for which clinicians report using AI – asking clinical questions, interpreting patient results, creating patient educational materials - could contribute substantially to healthcare outcomes if widely adopted. Designers of continuing education for clinicians should help provide opportunities for clinicians to improve their familiarity, use, and competency with AI tools, to help maximize the potential health benefits possible for patients and communities.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Objective: The aim of this study was to evaluate the effect of artificial intelligence (AI) assistance on examination efficiency and ergonomics during cardiac sonography. Materials and Methods: Randomized, cross-over study design was used with an ultrasound equipment system, cardiovascular software, and integrated AI features. A cohort of experienced sonographers (N = 30) performed standardized examinations with and without AI features enabled. All participating sonographers were new equipment users. Metrics of timing with and without AI assistance were acquired. Movements of the non-scanning hand were recorded during a subset of studies to assess time spent in a predefined ergonomic zone. Results: Artificial intelligence assistance reduced mean examination time by 10.16 ± 0.95 minutes (95% CI, 12.10-8.22; P < .001) independent of experience, age, scanning sequence, or prior AI familiarity. A sub-analysis of hand motion during sonography (n = 9) found AI assistance reduced average distance traveled by 50% (47.9 m) compared with unassisted examinations (SD, 10.6; 95% CI, 39.74-55.97, P < .01). Conclusion: In this cohort of users, AI-assisted cardiac sonography significantly reduced acquisition time and increased time spent within their optimal hand reach. This kind of upgrade may help lower the risk of work-related musculoskeletal injuries in cardiac sonographers. Further studies, based on actual clinical settings, would help to further clarify these benefits.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly shaping assessment practices in higher education through tools such as automated grading systems, AI-generated feedback, learning analytics, and technologies designed to detect academic dishonesty. While these innovations promise greater efficiency, scalability, and consistency in evaluating student performance, they also introduce significant challenges related to fairness, transparency, academic integrity, and institutional governance. This chapter argues that the central challenge of AI-mediated assessment is not purely technological but lies in the governance of trust within assessment systems. Furthermore, it examines how AI reshapes power relations among educators, students, institutions, and technological systems, while highlighting issues such as algorithmic bias, surveillance-oriented integrity technologies, and unequal global adoption of AI.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: BackgroundHairdressers are exposed to various occupational hazards, including musculoskeletal disorders, respiratory issues, and dermatological conditions due to prolonged standing, repetitive hand movements, and frequent contact with chemicals.ObjectiveThis study aims to assess the level of knowledge among hairdressers in Kayseri regarding occupational risk factors, determine the incidence of occupational health problems, and examine associated factors.MethodsThe study was conducted in Kayseri, Türkiye, with the participation of 286 hairdressers of both genders who provide services to women.The questionnaire consisted of 65 items divided into three constructs: sociodemographic characteristics (age, gender, education, work experience), work-related factors (work organization, PPE usage, occupational risk perception), and occupational health indicators (musculoskeletal, skin, respiratory symptoms, and general health status).ResultsAmong hairdressers, 54.5% experienced musculoskeletal symptoms, while 18.2% reported contact dermatitis symptoms and 19.6% had work-related asthma symptoms. Longer years of work experience and prolonged standing hours were found to increase ergonomic complaints.ConclusionsHairdressers with a history of atopy or precursor symptoms such as rhinitis and conjunctivitis should be screened for asthma. Ergonomic arrangements that will shorten long standing working times can reduce musculoskeletal complaints. Regular health screenings and preventive measures should be implemented to identify and manage at-risk individuals early.
topics: Occupational Health and Safety in Workplaces

documents.abstract: Safety-aligned large language models (LLMs) remain vulnerable to jailbreaks and can over-refuse benign requests. Understanding these failures requires distinguishing harmfulness recognition from the computation that writes refusal. We reframe this as a pathway question and make it measurable on residual-stream updates in decoder-only Transformers, separating the harmfulness information a module update exposes from the change it produces in readable refusal evidence. Across 18 Base-Instruct pairs spanning Qwen, Llama, and Gemma, harmfulness is decoded more readily from attention updates, particularly in early layers, whereas MLP updates contribute more strongly to harm-selective refusal writing in aligned models. Post-training strengthens MLP refusal writing in all 18 pairs without systematically improving harmfulness decodability, while positive MLP writing becomes more concentrated in deeper layers after post-training. Across six reasoning-enabled models, harmfulness remains decodable during reasoning while strong refusal writing concentrates at answer onset, a pattern that persists with reasoning disabled. Causal interventions further support this pathway: resetting downstream MLP updates to their clean values substantially reduces the refusal shift caused by upstream attention interventions. Building on these findings, we introduce Sentinel, which combines an attention-derived perception score P with an MLP-derived decision score D. Their joint profiles characterize jailbreaks and over-refusals, and conditional routing with both signals achieves a lower aggregate error rate than single-signal routing and evaluated fixed reminders across eight models.

Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has destabilised conventional assessment arrangements in higher education by lowering the cost of producing plausible academic texts and solutions. In this context, institutional responses have frequently concentrated on detection and surveillance, or on narrow policy prohibitions, approaches that risk eroding trust, amplifying inequities, and misrecognising assessment as a socio-pedagogical practice shaped by institutional cultures, disciplinary norms, and unequal access to resources. This chapter advances a theoretically informed redesign agenda that re-centres authentic assessment and assessment-for-learning (AfL) as complementary foundations for quality and integrity in AI-rich environments. Rather than treating GenAI as an external threat to be “controlled,” the chapter conceptualises GenAI as a socio-technical mediator within learners' activity systems and academic literacies, requiring assessment designs that make learning processes visible, uphold fairness and accountability, and preserve students' epistemic agency.

Assessment plays a pivotal contentious role in language education, in African contexts, where colonial-era epistemologies and monolingual standards have shaped prevailing practices. Assessment frameworks for African languages often mirror those designed for dominant global languages, neglecting learners' sociolinguistic realities. Concurrently, the rise of generative artificial intelligence tools has catalysed discussions about academic integrity and assessment validity, in English-medium higher education. This chapter addresses a significant gap in the discourse on African languages and generative AI by examining how authentic assessment and assessment for learning can be redefined in these contexts. The chapter suggests that GenAI can serve as a transformative catalyst that challenges conventional definitions of knowledge, performance, and learning. By foregrounding ethical, linguistic, and epistemic concerns unique to Africa, this chapter aims to contribute insights into the pedagogical possibilities of decoloniality that emerge when integrating AI into African language education.

Ventriculomegaly (VM) is one of the most common central nervous system (CNS) abnormalities, with important associations with other congenital defects, chromosomal abnormalities, and intrauterine infections. Accurate measurement of ventricular width is crucial for prenatal diagnosis and risk assessment. However, the operator-dependent nature of ultrasound introduces measurement variability, which can impact diagnostic accuracy. Although artificial intelligence (AI) has shown potential in ultrasound analysis, its performance in automated VM assessment and its agreement with radiologists with varying levels of expertise remain limitation. This study aims to develop a deep learning framework for automated measurement and diagnosis of fetal VM and evaluate its clinical applicability by comparing its performance with radiologists with varying levels of expertise. In this study, we collected ultrasound data from 1,018 fetuses across 4 hospitals to develop and evaluate a deep learning framework for automated fetal VM assessment. Images from normal fetuses and fetuses with VM were randomly assigned (ratio, 4:1) to training and internal validation datasets. An independent dataset was used for external validation and comparison with radiologists with different levels of expertise. We evaluated two automated strategies: landmark localization (AI-LandVM) and segmentation-based measurement (AI-SegVM), using a U-Net architecture to estimate lateral ventricular width. Diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, measurement error, and Bland–Altman analysis were used to evaluate the performance of the AI framework and compare it with radiologists with varying levels of experience. The AI-SegVM framework achieved high diagnostic performance, with an accuracy of 98.20%, and demonstrated excellent agreement with expert annotations, achieving a mean absolute error (MAE) of $$0.53\pm1.17$$ mm and an intra-class correlation coefficient (ICC) of 93.02%. Compared with radiologists with different levels of expertise, AI-SegVM showed lower measurement variability and consistent diagnostic performance. In contrast, the AI-LandVM strategy exhibited inferior performance, likely due to its limited ability to capture comprehensive ventricular structural information. The AI-SegVM framework provides a reliable approach for automated fetal VM measurement and diagnosis, demonstrating potential to reduce operator-dependent variability and support standardized prenatal ultrasound assessment. These findings highlight the potential of AI-assisted approaches for improving the consistency and efficiency of fetal VM evaluation.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Triage of rheumatology outpatient referrals is a high-volume administrative task that consumes senior specialist time without advancing patient care. The human triage system is only moderately accurate and reproducible. We assessed whether contemporary large language models (LLMs) are able to perform well enough to support automating this task in practice. In addition, the effects of different prompting techniques on triage accuracy and cost was assessed to help identify the optimal approach. Twenty referral scenarios spanning the urgency spectrum were created by a certified Australian rheumatologist. Four rheumatologists triaged all cases independently and blinded to produce a consensus reference standard; inter-rater reliability was quantified. Twenty-three LLMs each triaged every referral into one of five urgency categories, three times (1380 outputs per referral). The experiment was run with a simple prompt and repeated with an advanced prompt supplying explicit triage expectations and worked examples. In line with published literature, agreement among the four rheumatologists was moderate (Fleiss kappa 0.60; mean pairwise linear-weighted kappa 0.79), with all four assigning categories within one level of each other in 90% of cases. All 2760 model calls returned an interpretable result. Under the simple prompt, performance separated into distinct tiers, larger models were more accurate (Spearman rho = 0.42; P=.047) and accuracy tracked cost. Advanced prompting reduced between-model variance in accuracy 5.3-fold (0.014 to 0.003; Levene P=.01), abolished the size-accuracy association (rho=-0.05; P=.83) and removed the accuracy-cost relationship. The best models matched expert consensus on 18 of 20 cases, comparable to the reproducibility observed among the rheumatologists themselves. Under-triage errors persisted with some LLMs. Contemporary LLMs categorised rheumatology referral urgency with an accuracy and reproducibility comparable to that reported for human triage systems, although human triage was not tested in this study. Advanced prompting appeared to substitute for the reasoning capability of larger models, suggesting that adequate performance on this task may not require the most expensive models. These findings indicate that automation of this administrative task is technically feasible. Candidate models that warrant prospective evaluation are identified.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Abstract—The transition from static, single-prompt Large Language Models (LLMs) toward autonomous agentic architectures represents a major paradigm shift in artificial intelligence and computer systems engineering. Modern autonomous agents perceive, reason, formulate multi-step plans, invoke dynamic tools via application programming interfaces (APIs), and iteratively correct operational trajectories. When orchestrated into Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), these discrete cognitive units achieve collaborative problem-solving capabilities far exceeding individual models. However, realizing reliable MAS deployments introduces severe challenges in multi-agent consensus protocols, cognitive memory hierarchies, cascading hallucination mitigation, token consumption economics, and execution safety. This paper presents an exhaustive technical survey and rigorous architectural synthesis of contemporary agentic AI frameworks—including LangGraph, AutoGen, CrewAI, and MetaGPT. We formalize agent cognitive workflows as Partially Observable Markov Decision Processes (POMDPs) augmented by Tree-of-Thought (ToT) deliberation, analyze inter-agent communication topologies (hierarchical, peer-to-peer peer-review, and blackboard memory sharing), and formulate distributed consensus models under stochastic inference noise. Furthermore, we conduct a standardized empirical benchmark across four mission-critical domains (complex software synthesis, strategic decision-making, automated vulnerability discovery, and enterprise analytics). Our quantitative findings demonstrate that while hierarchical agent orchestrations achieve up to 34.8% higher task success rates over baseline chain-of-thought prompting, unconstrained peer-to-peer communications suffer exponential token overhead and vulnerability to deadlock. Finally, we formulate open research questions regarding mechanistic interpretability in agent negotiation, formal safety boundary verifications, and post-quantum cryptographic communication guarantees. Index Terms—Agentic AI, Autonomous Agents, Multi-Agent Systems (MAS), Foundation Models, Consensus Protocols, LangGraph, AutoGen, MetaGPT, Dynamic Replanning, Tool Augmented Generation.

Pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma (PDAC) remains one of the most challenging malignancies due to profound biological heterogeneity, complex stromal organization, and limited responsiveness to current immunotherapies. Recent advances in single-cell sequencing, spatial omics, digital pathology, and multimodal profiling have revealed that PDAC immune states are shaped not only by cellular composition but also by spatial organization, treatment context, and patient-specific evolutionary trajectories. However, the increasing complexity and fragmentation of biomedical evidence create substantial challenges for conventional artificial intelligence (AI) approaches that are typically optimized for predefined analytical tasks. Autonomous AI research agents represent an emerging paradigm that extends beyond predictive modeling by integrating scientific reasoning, retrieval of heterogeneous biomedical knowledge, computational tool orchestration, workflow adaptation, and evidence traceability. In this Review, we examine how agentic AI systems may contribute to PDAC immunology research, from characterization of immune ecosystems and spatial cellular interactions to biomarker discovery, neoantigen prioritization, and experimental protocol design. We distinguish AI agents from conventional task-specific models and discuss essential capabilities required for reliable biomedical research, including planning, tool use, verification, memory, provenance tracking, and human oversight. Despite promising technical demonstrations in biomedical domains, direct evidence supporting fully autonomous AI-driven discovery and validation in PDAC remains limited. Therefore, we propose a disease-oriented evaluation framework emphasizing benchmark task design, appropriate human and computational comparators, reproducibility assessment, and experimental validation. Future PDAC-specific AI research agents should prioritize evidence-aware reasoning, multimodal integration, calibrated uncertainty, and transparent computational–experimental workflows. Such systems may ultimately accelerate mechanistic discovery and precision immunology, while maintaining rigorous standards for biological validity, reproducibility, and responsible scientific practice.

documents.abstract: The rapid evolution of Industry 4.0 and 5.0 demands flexible manufacturing systems that move beyond traditional rigid automation. This paper presents an integrated framework for Autonomous Mobile Manipulators (AMMs) driven by Edge Artificial Intelligence (AI) and advanced computer vision. By combining simultaneous localization and mapping (SLAM) with multi-axis force-torque sensing, the proposed system bridges the gap between autonomous mobility and precise robotic manipulation. Experimental evaluations in a simulated smart-factory environment demonstrate a 31% reduction in component transfer time, zero safety incidents during close human-cobot interactions, and a 96% first-attempt pick success rate for variable parts. This study highlights the viability of deploying collaborative mobile manipulators to achieve highly adaptable, human-centric production lines.

The growing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) audits has created new opportunities to enhance corporate governance through faster and more consistent assurance processes. However, concerns remain regarding accountability, transparency, and the role of human oversight in AI-assisted auditing. Prior research has predominantly examined AI adoption in traditional financial auditing, leaving its role in the more qualitative and judgment-intensive context of ESG assurance comparatively underexplored, particularly with respect to how AI decision-making authority should be balanced against human oversight. This study examines the effects of AI automation and AI decision making on audit efficiency, accountability, and transparency, while assessing the mediating role of human oversight. A quantitative research design was adopted, and data were collected from 150 professionals involved in ESG audit-related functions (including ESG auditors, compliance officers, sustainability managers, and AI governance analysts) across private, public, and non-governmental organizations, recruited through purposive and snowball sampling via professional networks, audit forums, and LinkedIn ESG groups. The data were analyzed using partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM). The findings indicate that AI automation significantly improves audit efficiency, accountability, and transparency. Similarly, AI decision making within governance structures exerts positive effects on all three outcome dimensions. Furthermore, human oversight partially mediates these relationships, strengthening the overall impact of AI on ESG audit outcomes. These results suggest that AI enhances ESG auditing effectiveness, but its benefits are maximized when supported by strong governance and human supervision. The study contributes to the emerging literature on AI-enabled ESG assurance by demonstrating the importance of balancing technological efficiency with accountability and transparency in corporate governance.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Abstract The emergence of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) has prompted universities to develop policies regulating its use in teaching, learning, and assessment. Little empirical research has examined how they conceptualise assessment, and the assumptions underpinning their normative frameworks. This study addresses this gap through a comparative analysis of GenAI-related policy documents from 14 universities in Switzerland and Spain. Drawing on Chan's AI Ecological Education Policy Framework and Bacchi's problematisation theory, we use collaborative consensus-based coding to examine pedagogical, governance, and operational dimensions alongside problem representations, assumptions, subject positions, and silences. The findings reveal coexisting and sometimes competing representations of GenAI. Concerns about academic integrity, authorship, transparency, and data protection coexist with calls for AI literacy, assessment redesign, formative feedback, and critical engagement with AI. Assessment emerges as a key site of this tension, with policies combining AI-resistant approaches with attempts to integrate GenAI into educational processes. The analysis also reveals asymmetrical subject positions: teachers and institutions generally define legitimate AI use, whereas students are positioned as accountable users expected to disclose, justify, or verify their use of AI. AI literacy and evaluative judgement are likewise framed mainly as students competencies, leaving teachers corresponding needs less examined. Current GenAI policy therefore represent an important but incomplete response to AI-driven change. Future policy development should move beyond regulating acceptable use towards participatory and pedagogically grounded frameworks that involve students more actively in shaping AI-mediated assessment and support human agency, evaluative judgement, and meaningful learning.

Abstract Individual consent, while essential to privacy and informational autonomy, is insufficient to govern artificial intelligence systems that generate collective harms, extract collective value, and process culturally sensitive knowledge. This paper examines the limitations of individual-centred privacy governance and advances a framework for Indigenous AI sovereignty grounded in collective authority, community protocol, and enforceable control throughout the AI lifecycle. Drawing on First Nations' OCAP principles, the CARE Principles for Indigenous Data Governance, the United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples, and relevant Canadian and international AI governance frameworks, the paper examines the relationship between data sovereignty, digital infrastructure, cultural representation, and downstream technological use. Its central contribution is a proposed Indigenous AI Sovereignty Audit designed to evaluate whether collective rights are translated into operational governance. The framework addresses community authority, secondary-use restrictions, data possession, provenance, derivative AI artifacts, benefit-sharing, cultural safety, and mechanisms for challenge and redress. The paper argues that meaningful Indigenous AI sovereignty requires more than consent to data collection. It requires the continuing ability of Indigenous peoples and their legitimate governing institutions to determine how information is used, transformed, commercialized, and represented through artificial intelligence. Publication note: Independent research working paper. Research and source review current as of 10 April 2026. This manuscript has not been represented as peer-reviewed.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: Artificial Intelligence (AI) is reshaping assessment in higher education by enhancing efficiency, scalability, and personalized feedback. However, its growing use raises critical ethical concerns regarding academic integrity, fairness, transparency, accountability, privacy, and trust. This chapter explores how AI can be integrated into assessment while maintaining educational values. Drawing on the Responsible Innovation (RI) framework, it reframes AI-mediated assessment as an ethical governance challenge rather than a purely technological issue. An integrative literature review synthesizes current scholarship on AI in assessment, highlighting both opportunities and risks. Findings highlight the importance of robust governance, human oversight, stakeholder engagement, transparent policies, and continuous evaluation of algorithmic impacts. The chapter argues that responsible AI adoption is essential for promoting fair, inclusive, and trustworthy assessment practices in higher education.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT BACKGROUND Fraud vulnerability is an increasing concern in aging populations, particularly as financial activities shift to digital environments. Individuals with neurocognitive disorders may be especially vulnerable, yet the relative contribution of financial literacy, behavioral functioning, neuropsychiatric symptoms, and interpersonal factors remains poorly understood. This study examined these determinants in individuals with neurocognitive disorders. METHODS 290 individuals with neurocognitive disorders, including Alzheimer’s disease, frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia, semantic dementia, and mild cognitive impairment, were enrolled. Financial vulnerability was assessed using the Financial Frailty Battery, a caregiver-administered instrument evaluating financial behaviors before and after disease onset. Neuropsychiatric symptoms were assessed with the Neuropsychiatric Inventory. Regression models examined predictors of fraud occurrence, fraud type, and fraud frequency. RESULTS Behavioral changes in everyday functioning and interpersonal trust emerged as the strongest correlates of fraud vulnerability. Behavioral tendencies (OR = 1.10, 95% CI [1.01, 1.19], p = .030) and trust (OR = 1.11, 95% CI [1.04, 1.18], p < .001) significantly predicted fraud victimization. Higher trust predicted non-digital (OR = 1.12, p = .005) and mixed fraud (OR = 1.19, p < .001), but not digital-only fraud (OR = 1.08, p = .101). Trust was also associated with repeated victimization (χ 2 (2) = 42.2, p < .001). CONCLUSIONS Fraud vulnerability in neurocognitive disorders appears to be driven primarily by behavioral and interpersonal factors rather than financial knowledge alone. Preliminary evidence suggests partially different vulnerability profiles for digital and non-digital fraud, highlighting the need for prevention strategies tailored to different forms of financial exploitation.

Contemporary implant dentistry achieves remarkable survival rates, yet the rising prevalence of peri-implantitis and increasing patient complexity reveal the limits of a technically centered model. This narrative review synthesizes current evidence supporting the four pillars of the 4P framework—predictive, preventive, personalized, and participatory—and proposes an integrated patient-centered clinical algorithm for implant dentistry. Throughout this review, “4P” is used as the preferred designation; “P4 medicine” appears only in direct citation of original systems-medicine sources. A narrative literature search was conducted in PubMed, Scopus, and the Cochrane Library (January 2000 to June 2026). Reporting followed Scale for the Assessment of Narrative Review Articles (SANRA) Predictive tools—resonance frequency analysis, genomic biomarkers [investigational], artificial intelligence algorithms, and radiomic analysis—contribute to individual risk stratification, with variable levels of clinical validation. Preventive strategies anchored in a four-level continuum are associated with a peri-implantitis frequency of 18% in maintenance-compliant patients versus 43.9% in non-compliant patients, illustrating the measurable clinical impact of the preventive pillar. Personalized approaches optimize osseointegration according to each patient’s biological profile. Participatory implantology, through shared decision-making and patient-reported outcome measures, improves the therapeutic alliance and long-term adherence. The 4P model constitutes a coherent and clinically applicable conceptual framework. Its novel contribution is a sequential decision-making logic distinguishing pre-placement gate-keeping from post-placement dynamic pillar reorientation, providing clinicians with a structured conceptual framework applicable at each phase of implant treatment.

The current paradigm of artificial intelligence (AI) design elevates conversational chatbot interfaces, making them the default mode through which hundreds of millions of people interact with AI systems globally. This narrative review identifies three related harms produced by the single-voice chatbot interface, drawing on insights from literature in cognitive science, political studies, AI alignment, game design and human computer interaction. Firstly, cognitive offloading of user thinking, secondly, ideological narrowing of user beliefs, and thirdly, epistemic compression of cultural and value diversity. We then propose multi-persona interfaces, in which multiple personas are presented to the user simultaneously, as a cost-effective intervention that addresses all three harms at once. We ground this intervention in traditions the AI literature has largely overlooked, drawing on techniques from game design and participatory simulation, including the magic circle, role differentiation, and persona embodiment. We propose a taxonomy for the future design of multi-persona interfaces, and call for a research agenda that closes the gap between technical pluralistic alignment methods and empirical studies of human-AI interactions with pluralistic interfaces.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: The rapid diffusion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is prompting a critical reconsideration of established assessment practices in foreign language education. This paper argues that a continued reliance on written assessment, increasingly vulnerable to the unauthorised use of AI-enabled technologies and personal devices, may undermine the validity of language assessment. Drawing on the principles underlying ALTE guidelines and the Common European Framework of Reference for Languages (CEFR), the article challenges the widespread assumption that standardised written testing necessarily provides a more objective measure of linguistic competence. It argues instead for a renewed centrality of oral performance, which enables teachers to observe learners’ linguistic resources and communicative competence in real time. Oral assessment, when supported by clearly defined criteria and appropriately designed tasks, offers a particularly direct means of assessing spontaneous language use, interaction and the negotiation of meaning. The paper also addresses practical and psychological concerns associated with oral assessment, particularly its implementation in large classes and its relationship with foreign language anxiety. It concludes that the emergence of GenAI should not simply be regarded as a threat to academic integrity, but as a catalyst for rethinking assessment practices and restoring greater importance to forms of evaluation that privilege authentic, synchronous and interpersonal language use.

documents.abstract: Digitalization in dentistry signifies a new era that goes beyond transferring imaging, impression-taking, design, and manufacturing stages to computer-aided systems and requires biological characteristics, clinical findings, patient preferences, and long-term risks to be evaluated within a shared data model. In this chapter, “biodigital dentistry” is defined as the integration of patients’ clinical, radiological, morphological, functional, and, when necessary, molecular data through digital technologies and the use of this integrated information in diagnosis, treatment simulation, interdisciplinary sequencing, manufacturing, and monitoring processes. The historical development of the transition from conventional to digital workflows, virtual patient creation, clinical–radiological–digital data fusion, artificial intelligence-assisted decision-support systems, the timing of periodontal–orthodontic–surgical–restorative treatments, and personalized care models are discussed in light of current evidence. Ethical and legal issues, including algorithmic bias, explainability, data minimization, cybersecurity, informed consent, and the domestic and international transfer of health data, are also evaluated in terms of clinical applicability. The principal objective of the biodigital transformation is not to replace the clinician but to facilitate more predictable decision-making for the right patient, at the right time, and within biological limits. Successful implementation requires an interoperable data infrastructure, validated technologies, shared interdisciplinary objectives, human oversight, and continuous outcome monitoring.
topics: Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare and Education

documents.abstract: Background/Objectives: Orthodontic treatment response varies considerably among patients because mechanical loading interacts with individual biological, anatomical, systemic, and behavioral characteristics. Advances in mechanobiology, molecular biomarkers, omics technologies, and artificial intelligence (AI) may support a more personalized approach to treatment. This systematic review (SR) aimed to evaluate human clinical evidence concerning these domains and their potential contribution to predicting orthodontic response, improving clinical decision-making, and reducing adverse effects. Methods: A systematic search of PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science was conducted through June 2026. Primary studies involving human participants and addressing orthodontic tooth movement (OTM), biological variability, biomarkers, genomics, epigenetics, multi-omics, or AI-supported orthodontics were selected according to predefined eligibility criteria. The review was conducted and reported in accordance with Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) 2020, and heterogeneous evidence was synthesized narratively across four predefined domains. The review protocol was registered in the International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews (PROSPERO; registration number CRD420261486348). Risk of bias was assessed using design-appropriate instruments. Certainty of evidence was assessed at the outcome level using GRADE principles adapted to narrative synthesis. Results: The search identified 1051 records, of which 14 primary human studies were included. The clinical evidence comprised randomized trials, longitudinal and cross-sectional biomarker studies, genetic association studies, and a case report. Molecular and multi-omics studies identified candidate markers of biological response and patient phenotype. The included computational studies examined genetic association rules, gingival-enlargement classification, and AI-assisted root-resorption measurement; none demonstrated AI-guided selection of orthodontic forces. However, small samples, methodological heterogeneity, limited adjustment for confounding, and lack of external validation restricted clinical translation. Certainty of evidence supporting clinical personalization applications was predominantly very low. Conclusions: Personalized orthodontics should remain grounded in comprehensive diagnosis, biologically compatible mechanics, and individualized monitoring. Molecular and computational tools may complement clinical assessment, but routine implementation requires standardized protocols, multicenter validation, and prospective evidence of patient-relevant benefit.

ABSTRACT Blockchain introduced secure, peer‐to‐peer transactions in decentralized environments without reliance on central authorities. However, attackers continue to exploit blockchain projects. Over the past decade, reported blockchain exploit losses have exceeded $24 billion. Although existing research analyzes blockchain vulnerabilities and real‐world incidents, many studies focus on specific vulnerability classes or smart contract issues only. Therefore, we present an empirical study of major blockchain exploits from 2020 to 2025. Based on detailed analysis of these exploits, we introduce a practitioner‐oriented taxonomy that organizes the dominant root causes observed in the analyzed exploits across four domains: Human Risks, Off‐Chain Infrastructure Vulnerabilities, Private Key Compromises, and Smart Contract Vulnerabilities. Across these categories, we present case studies, code illustrations where applicable, and mitigation strategies. Moreover, we evaluate five vulnerability‐detection tools spanning four paradigms, namely static analysis ( Slither , 4naly3er ), symbolic execution ( Mythril ), bounded/formal verification ( SMTChecker ), and LLM‐assisted analysis ( GPTScan ), on a curated test suite of vulnerable and secure contracts. Our results show detection gaps under the evaluated setting: Slither, Mythril, and 4naly3er all scored recall below 40%. SMTChecker and GPTScan were evaluated separately because of their narrower target scopes. SMTChecker detected only arithmetic issues, while GPTScan produced no benchmark‐relevant detections. The study highlights the high average loss associated with smart contract access‐control failures, the need for post‐deployment monitoring beyond one‐time audits, and risks related to Off‐Chain Infrastructure Vulnerabilities. By analyzing exploits and offering mitigations, we provide a structured reference for identifying, prioritizing, and mitigating major blockchain security risks.

documents.abstract: Background: Global STEM reforms increasingly privilege technical proficiency while sidelining moral teleology, leaving graduates adept with code but adrift on questions of purpose. This study advances a Scripture‑anchored, interdisciplinary framework that reunites scientific inquiry with a Christian worldview and empirically tests its influence on student learning. Methodology: Adopting a qualitative‑dominant mixed‑methods design, we executed an AI‑assisted meta‑synthesis of 180 peer‑reviewed sources (2019‑2025) and triangulated those insights with multi‑site case studies of Wheaton College (USA), Daystar University (Kenya), and Redeemer University (Canada). Data—curricula, alumni surveys, and classroom artefacts—underwent thematic coding and cross‑case pattern matching, generating testable propositions linking faith‑based instruction, epistemic coherence, and learning outcomes. Results: Across contexts, faith‑integrated STEM programmes exhibited markedly greater cognitive engagement, deeper ethical reasoning, and heightened spiritual formation than secular comparators. Meta‑synthesised effect sizes (Hedges g = 0.35–0.55) show that explicit biblical framing elevates moral‑reasoning and purpose metrics, with the most pronounced gains among students previously unfamiliar with faith‑learning integration. Key mediators include faculty integration skill, mission‑aligned accreditation standards, and culturally attuned pedagogy. Conclusions: Positioning sola Scriptura as the ultimate epistemic authority does not dilute scientific rigour; it re‑humanises STEM by welding empirical facts to transcendent purpose. The proposed framework supplies educators, policymakers, and accreditation bodies with a scalable roadmap for producing technically competent, ethically resilient graduates equipped to steward AI, biotechnology, and green‑tech frontiers. Future research should deploy longitudinal, multi‑institutional designs and neurocognitive measures to further validate the model’s causal pathways and global applicability.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is transforming graduate research and academic work; however, increased use does not necessarily lead to critical evaluation or responsible engagement. This study examines the gap between graduate students’ AI use and their evaluative, ethical, and rhetorical engagement with AI-generated outputs. Using a survey-based exploratory case study design, the study draws on data from 50 graduate students across four national contexts, complemented by open-ended responses and contextual observations. Findings reveal high levels of AI use alongside limited verification practices, ethical uncertainty, and a tendency to view AI outputs as neutral or authoritative, indicating a persistent use–competence gap. The study proposes a holistic AI literacy framework with implications for curriculum, assessment, and policy.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

documents.abstract: CAD/CAM technologies have transformed the production of fixed prosthodontic restorations from a craft based on manual skill into a standardized and measurable digital process. This chapter addresses, for dental students in their clinical years and for early-career clinicians, the fundamental principles of CAD/CAM systems, digital and artificial intelligence-assisted restoration design, milling and three-dimensional printing technologies, contemporary restorative materials, the factors influencing material selection, accuracy and quality control in digital manufacturing, and the biocompatible and smart materials of the future, in the light of the current and verified literature. The digital workflow comprises three interdependent links—data acquisition, design, and manufacturing—and the quality of the final restoration is limited by the weakest link in the chain. Although milling remains the gold standard for definitive restorations, additive manufacturing has become established for interim restorations, models, and surgical guides, and it is a rapidly maturing alternative for definitive restorations. On the material side, the rise of monolithic zirconia, the diversification of lithium silicate glass-ceramics, and the establishment of resin-matrix ceramics in minimally invasive applications offer the clinician a broad range of options with varying levels of evidence. Current systematic-review and meta-analytic evidence shows that AI-assisted design shortens design time and improves reproducibility, but that human oversight remains indispensable. Clinical success depends on manufacturing the right material with validated parameters for the right indication and applying it with an appropriate adhesive or conventional cementation protocol. Accuracy should be defined by its trueness and precision components, marginal fit should be evaluated against clinical acceptability thresholds, and quality control should be maintained at every link of the digital chain. The graded, bioactive, self-healing, and stimuli-responsive materials of the future, together with additively manufactured ceramics, signal a transition from passive to smart materials in restorative dentistry.
